scenes.label: 01 / THE DOCUMENT
scenes.title: The Man Who Never Existed
text: The first thing Javis noticed was the date.
He stared at the document on his computer screen.
The university archives were quiet except for the low hum of the ventilation system. Outside, rain struck the windows in irregular bursts, blurring the distant lights of the city.
Javis leaned closer to the monitor.
The document had appeared in the restricted archive twenty minutes earlier. No sender. No authorization signature. No record of its creation.
His name was uncommon, but not unique.
The first page contained a photograph of a young man lying on a metal examination table.
He recognized the scar above his left eyebrow.
He recognized the silver chain around his neck.
Beneath the photograph were three lines.
Because the alternative was to believe it.

scenes.label: 02 / THE KNOCK
scenes.title: The Other Voice
text: Twenty-seven minutes later, the archive lights went out.
They disappeared one after another, beginning at the far end of the corridor.
Something moved beyond the glass door.
He could not see its face.
Then the emergency lights came on.
Now the image showed Javis standing in the archive, staring at his computer.
The photograph had been taken from behind him.
He didn't want to open it.
This photograph showed the archive door.
And standing in the doorway was a man wearing Javis's face.
Beneath the photograph was a single sentence.

text.terminal: THE FIRST VERSION HAS ALREADY BEEN REPLACED.

text: And a voice, identical to his own, whispered:
For several seconds, the only sound was rain against the windows.
The voice had come from the other side.
The archive was locked from the inside, and he was the only person authorized to work after midnight.
He took one step toward the door.
A sharp knock made him flinch.
His voice, down to the slight roughness that appeared when he was tired.
“Listen carefully,” it said. “You have very little time.”
Javis looked toward the security monitor mounted beside his desk.
The corridor camera showed an empty hallway.
The camera inside the archive showed him standing near the desk.
There was a thin cut across his palm.
A few minutes earlier, he'd been sorting a box of damaged manuscripts. One of the metal fasteners must have caught his skin.
Javis felt something cold settle in his stomach.
“Three years ago, you told Professor Thorne that you hated working with people because books couldn't disappoint you.”
“You didn't mean it. You were angry because he'd rejected your application for the research fellowship.”
His eyes moved toward the bottom drawer of his desk.
He hadn't opened that drawer in months.
“Under the old photographs,” the voice added.
He had no idea why he'd said it.
Perhaps because he wanted the stranger to prove that this was some elaborate prank.
Perhaps because part of him wanted to see the face.
“If I open it, they'll know which one survived.”
A low mechanical hum rose from somewhere beneath the floor.
Then the voice said something that made Javis forget the door entirely.
“Ask yourself why you can't remember your mother's face.”

scenes.label: 03 / THE MEMORY
scenes.title: No Valid History
text: That was the first thing Javis thought.
He remembered a woman standing in a garden, smiling beneath the afternoon sun.
He remembered her hands adjusting the collar of his school uniform.
He remembered the smell of something warm baking in a kitchen.
But when he tried to picture her face, the memory refused to settle.
The harder he concentrated, the less certain it became.
He pressed his fingers against his temples.
He'd lost his parents when he was young. Memories faded. That was normal.
Still, he found himself reaching for his phone.
There was a photograph in his gallery. An old family portrait he'd scanned from a damaged print.
A small boy stood between two adults in front of a house.
The man beside him had dark hair and a serious expression.
Blurred in a perfect oval, as though someone had deliberately erased it.
The background remained sharp. Every leaf on the nearby tree was visible.
In every one, the woman's face was gone.
He opened his messaging app and searched for his mother's name.
Old university records appeared. A few administrative documents.
No photographs beyond the ones he'd saved.
“Listen to me. Whatever they've told you, don't believe—”
A harsh burst of static swallowed her words.
The number had disappeared from his call history.
Then the phone displayed a notification.
Beyond the door, his other self spoke again.
Javis looked at the blank security monitor.
He wasn't sure whether he was answering the stranger or himself.

scenes.label: 04 / THE MENTOR
scenes.title: Sixteen Previous Attempts
text: The thought came with such immediate certainty that Javis almost felt relieved.
Thorne had been his mentor for five years. He knew the university's archives better than anyone, including the restricted collections that most staff weren't permitted to enter.
More importantly, Thorne was the sort of man who could explain an impossible document without making its discovery feel like a personal failure.
“I found a document in the restricted archive. It has my name on it.”
The silence that followed was different.
Long enough for Javis to hear the rain striking the windows.
A faint noise came through the phone.
A chair scraping across a floor.
“Javis, listen carefully. Do not open that door.”
“Do not touch anything else in the archive.”
He hadn't asked whether Javis was joking.
Javis waited another minute before approaching the door.
He placed his ear against the glass.
Then he noticed something on the floor.
A narrow strip of paper had been pushed beneath the door.
He crouched and picked it up.
It was a library borrowing slip.
The university had stopped using paper slips decades ago.
Across the top, someone had written:
Below it was a handwritten message.
He knows more than he's told you.
Then he looked toward the computer.
The original case file was still open.
Beneath the photograph and termination record, a section had appeared that hadn't been there before.
The man who'd given him his first position at the university.
The man he'd just called for help.
A new line appeared beneath Thorne's name.
He thought of the case number.
One showed him lying beneath the wreckage of a collapsed building.
Another showed him strapped to a hospital bed.
A third showed him standing beside a woman whose face had been erased.
The final photograph was taken in the university archive.
And the body lying on the floor.
The photograph showed something that had supposedly happened thirty-six minutes ago.
Something he had no memory of.
Then a terrible possibility occurred to him.
He scrolled back to the top of the file.

scenes.label: 05 / THE OVERRIDE
scenes.title: The Professor and His Escort
text: Javis watched him through the corridor camera.
The professor wore a dark coat over his usual clothes. His silver hair was damp from the rain.
One carried a narrow metal case.
The other held a device that emitted a faint blue light.
Javis didn't recognize either of them.
His voice came through the intercom.
“There's been a serious breach. We need to make sure you're safe.”
Javis looked down at the borrowing slip.
He knows more than he's told you.
But Javis had known him long enough to notice.
For one brief moment, he looked exhausted.
Then he stepped closer to the camera.
“Javis, whatever you've found, you don't understand it.”
“I will. But first, open the door.”
“Because the longer you remain in there, the more dangerous this becomes.”
Javis looked toward the metal case.
One of the men whispered something to him.
“Javis, I need you to trust me.”
Five years of trust didn't disappear because of a strange document.
He remembered the professor helping him secure a scholarship when his funding collapsed.
He remembered the evenings they'd spent debating obscure historical records.
He remembered Thorne visiting him in hospital after an accident two years earlier.
The man had been more than a supervisor.
He'd been the closest thing Javis had to family.
And that was precisely why the next question hurt.
He had never heard Thorne say that before.
“You told me you'd never met them.”
Thorne glanced at the men beside him.
“Some truths are dangerous when discovered at the wrong time.”
Javis stepped away from the monitor.
The man with the metal case moved toward the door.
A thin instrument extended from the case and pressed against the electronic lock.

scenes.label: 06 / THE PASSAGE
scenes.title: The Forgotten Staircase
text: He didn't think about where he was going.
He simply turned and hurried between the archive shelves, past rows of sealed manuscripts and forgotten records.
The restricted collection occupied the oldest wing of the university library. Its shelves stretched into narrow corridors, some ending in locked storage rooms.
There was no second public exit.
He also knew there was a maintenance passage behind the preservation chamber.
Behind him, the archive entrance opened.
He reached the preservation chamber and pulled at the handle.
The third cabinet stood beside a damaged ventilation panel.
Inside were empty preservation boxes, a coil of cable, and a small brass key.
He pushed through the door and stumbled into darkness.
A narrow staircase descended beneath the library.
Javis switched on his phone's flashlight.
The walls were lined with old pipes.
Behind him, someone entered the preservation chamber.
The professor's voice carried genuine alarm.
For a moment, he considered turning back.

text.terminal: HE IS NOT AFRAID OF WHAT YOU WILL FIND.
HE IS AFRAID OF WHAT WILL REMEMBER YOU.

text: The maintenance door slammed shut behind him.
And something deep beneath the library began to hum.

scenes.label: 07 / THE ARTIFACT
scenes.title: What Remembers
text: The staircase ended at a steel door.
It was unlike anything Javis had seen in the university.
Its surface was smooth and dark, almost black, except for a faint circular pattern at its centre.
For an instant, the screen displayed a symbol he didn't recognize.
A vertical line through their centre.
Then the display returned to normal.
Its surface simply separated into countless thin lines that folded away from one another.
No signs that it belonged beneath a centuries-old library.
In the centre stood a stone pedestal.
And resting upon it was a black tablet.
The object was no larger than a book.
Its surface looked like polished obsidian, but something moved beneath it.
Thin lines of gold shifted through the darkness, forming symbols that dissolved before he could understand them.
He felt an inexplicable pressure behind his eyes.
If the world ever forgets you, find what remembers.
His phone vibrated one final time.
The voice seemed to rise from somewhere behind his thoughts.
Sixteen times, they have taken you from me.
The golden lines spread across the tablet.
Sixteen times, I have failed to keep you.
For a moment, the tablet reflected his face.
Then another face appeared beside it.
Professor Thorne standing over a body.
A violent impact shook the steel door behind him.
Thorne's voice echoed from the staircase.
Golden light spilled across the pedestal.
The door was beginning to open.
Beyond it stood Thorne and the two men.
He thought of the sixteen photographs.
The voice behind the archive door.
And the man he'd trusted for five years.
He placed his hand on the black surface.

scenes.label: 08 / THE OBSERVER
scenes.title: The Unregistered
text: Thorne stood motionless in the doorway, his mouth open around a warning that would never reach Javis.
Even the dust in the air had stopped moving.
Then a line of golden text appeared beneath his hand.
Javis stared at the final line.
The tablet did not answer immediately.
Instead, the golden symbols rearranged themselves.
A cold sensation passed through Javis.
For the first time since entering the chamber, he felt that something was watching him.
Not the men at the door.
Beyond the reality he had always believed was his own.
The tablet's voice returned, barely a whisper.
You are not the only one who remembers.
And somewhere beyond the stillness, something answered.

scenes.label: 09 / THE SECOND BETWEEN SECONDS
scenes.title: The Second Between Seconds
text: The first thing Javis noticed was the silence.
Not the familiar silence of the university archives, where the ventilation hummed behind the walls and rain tapped against the windows.
The dust had stopped falling. A fragment of plaster hung motionless above the floor. The emergency light over the chamber entrance remained caught between two flickers.
Professor Thorne stood in the doorway, one hand extended toward him. Frozen.
Behind the professor, two men occupied the narrow staircase. One held the blue-lit device Javis had seen on the security monitor.
Javis looked down at the black tablet beneath his hand.

text.terminal:
TEMPORAL DISPLACEMENT: ACTIVE
LOCAL CONTINUITY: SUSPENDED
EXTERNAL OBSERVER: PRESENT

text: He read the final line twice.
The answer still seemed to hang somewhere beyond the chamber.
His voice sounded wrong without an echo.

text.terminal:
OBSERVER IDENTITY: UNAVAILABLE
OBSERVER INFLUENCE: DETECTED
CONTACT STATUS: ESTABLISHED

text: Before he had touched the tablet? Before he had opened Case 0017?
He thought of the messages that had guided him through the archives. LEFT WALL. THIRD CABINET. YOU HAVE DONE THIS BEFORE.
Forty-seven seconds. Javis stopped asking questions.
He stepped toward the doorway. Thorne stood between him and the staircase, while the two men blocked the passage.

text.terminal:
REALITY ANCHOR DETECTED
TEMPORAL SUSPENSION EXEMPTION: ACTIVE

text: Whatever the men had brought operated under different rules. He did not want to discover those rules at close range.
He searched the chamber. Behind the pedestal, he found a seam almost invisible in the stone.
He pressed it. A section of wall withdrew, revealing a narrow maintenance passage.
Another hidden route. He could no longer tell whether the Codex was opening doors or simply helping him notice them.
He squeezed inside as the countdown reached its final seconds.
Through the opening, he saw a shadow appear on the chamber wall. There was no one standing where it should have originated.
Then time resumed. The ventilation roared. Plaster struck the floor.
Javis ran. He did not look back.

scenes.label: 10 / THE MAN IN THE PHOTOGRAPH
scenes.title: The Man in the Photograph
text: The passage climbed steeply before ending behind a service panel. Javis loosened two corroded bolts with his archive multitool and pushed through into a storage room.
Cleaning supplies. A wheeled trolley. An emergency lantern. Ordinary objects.
He had never been so relieved to see a mop.
His phone read 12:49 AM. He could not account for the missing time.
The photograph of Case 0017 remained on his phone.

text.terminal:
SUBJECT: JAVIS
CAUSE OF DEATH: DIMENSIONAL DISPLACEMENT
DATE OF TERMINATION: 17 OCTOBER — 02:14 AM

text: More than an hour remained. Unless the clock was lying.
He considered abandoning the tablet, then wrapped it in a cleaning cloth and kept it.
Footsteps approached. He ducked behind the trolley.
A guard and a maintenance worker entered, discussing the eastern corridor’s power failure.
“Third time this month,” the guard said.
When they left, he moved through the eastern wing toward the rear exit.
A wall-mounted monitor displayed a live security feed.
It showed him standing beside the screen.
Same height. Same build. Same face.
Javis spun around. The corridor was empty.
On the monitor, the other Javis raised a hand and pointed toward the exit.
Then words flashed across the image.
He had seen his double in photographs and heard his voice through a locked door. This one appeared to be responding to him.
Someone had been unable to see him until now.

scenes.label: 11 / THE HUNTERS
scenes.title: The Hunters
text: Rain fell steadily over the university grounds. A taxi passed beneath the streetlights. Somewhere, people were still living ordinary lives.

text.terminal:
DO NOT USE THE MAIN GATE.
THEY ARE WAITING FOR YOU.

text: A dark vehicle stood beyond the fence. Its headlights were off.

text.terminal: SOMEONE WHO WOULD PREFER YOU ALIVE.

text: He demanded proof. A photograph arrived showing him beneath a courtyard pillar, taken seconds earlier.
He challenged the sender to describe what lay behind the pillar.

text.terminal: BROKEN DRAINPIPE. THREE LOOSE BRICKS. EMPTY WATER BOTTLE.

text: A man in a dark suit stepped from the parked vehicle and turned directly toward him.
Javis ran through a staff gate and onto a service road. The man followed without appearing to hurry.
At the next junction, Javis turned into an alley.
A brick wall blocked the far end.
The man demanded the artifact. He claimed Professor Thorne was resolving an unfortunate situation.
“You’re not here to protect me,” Javis said.
The man reached into his coat.
Javis threw the wrapped tablet across the alley. The stranger looked toward it. Javis lunged past him.
A hand caught his jacket. Something cold touched the back of his neck.
The air became heavy. His muscles worked, but his body barely moved.
The stranger held a silver device with a pulsing blue centre.
The man approached the fallen tablet, then stopped. Its outline appeared doubled, as if two versions occupied the same place.
The stranger’s expression changed from composure to fear.
Behind Javis, the brick wall began to split.

scenes.label: 12 / THE DOOR THAT WASN’T THERE
scenes.title: The Door That Wasn’t There
text: Cracks spread across the wall in a pattern too precise to be damage. Straight lines. Perfect angles. A rectangle.
“Anchor integrity compromised,” the stranger said into his earpiece.
The blue light died. The pressure around Javis vanished.
He caught himself against the wall—and his hand passed through the brick.
“Do not enter that opening,” the stranger warned.
“Because you don’t know where it leads.”
A fair point. Then the man produced a second device.
For one impossible instant his body seemed to pull in several directions at once. Then he fell onto wet concrete in a different alley.
The university clock tower stood several blocks away.
He pressed a palm to the wall behind him. Solid brick.
The tablet was back in his jacket, although he had thrown it onto the pavement.

text.terminal:
SPATIAL TRANSITION: COMPLETED
DESTINATION: UNVERIFIED
CAUSAL INTEGRITY: DEGRADED

text: His shoulder hurt. His knees were scraped. He felt sick. Whatever had happened was not a convenient escape technique.
On the ground lay a wet black-and-white photograph.
It showed Javis in this alley, holding the tablet. Another Javis stood behind him, staring at something outside the frame with unmistakable terror.
On the reverse were four words.
“You really shouldn’t stand in the open like that,” a voice said.
A young man stood beneath a broken security light. Jeans. Dark jacket. Hands visible.
Kaelen urged him to move. Javis showed him the photograph.
Kaelen’s expression changed. “You found that here?”
Kaelen looked at the photograph. “Because that shouldn’t exist.”

scenes.label: 13 / THE WRONG QUESTION
scenes.title: The Wrong Question
text: Javis folded the photograph and slipped it into his pocket.
Javis stepped around him. Kaelen did not stop him.
“Seventeen October. Two fourteen in the morning. That’s when they expect you to disappear.”
Kaelen knew about the case and the previous versions. That did not make him trustworthy. It made him useful.
“For now, you walk in front,” Javis said.
“And keep your hands where I can see them.”
They moved through service roads, a pedestrian bridge, a closed pharmacy and an old railway underpass. Javis memorized each turn.
“How do you know Thorne?” he asked.
“He was my professor,” Javis continued. “He also appears to have supervised sixteen attempts to kill me.”
Javis did not move. “Start with one complete sentence.”
“The people hunting you aren’t trying to kill you.”
A train passed overhead. Kaelen waited for it to fade.
“Why they keep failing to make you stay dead.”
Javis felt the photograph in his pocket.
It was the first answer that sounded completely honest.
“But if they find you before then, they try again.”

scenes.label: 14 / A PLACE WITHOUT RECORDS
scenes.title: A Place Without Records
text: Kaelen led him to an abandoned municipal records office. The windows were boarded, the front door chained.
He entered a courtyard and opened a utility cabinet containing switches and a keypad. A section of wall slid inward.
“At least I’d know it was suspicious.”
Inside stood two desks, a worn sofa, a water dispenser and several monitors.
Kaelen locked the door. Javis checked for another exit.
“Emergency stairwell,” Kaelen said, pointing behind a curtain. “Leads to the roof.”
Javis placed the tablet on a desk but kept one hand close.
He asked what had happened when Javis touched the tablet.
Javis gave him a controlled account: the chamber, the frozen moment, the observer, the anchor, the changing feed and the impossible doorway.
He deliberately omitted the voice that had sounded like his own.
“Reality isn’t as fixed as people think.”
“Try explaining that without sounding like a philosophy lecturer.”
Kaelen drew a line across a sheet of paper, then another beside it.
“Most people experience one path. Cause, effect, time moving forward. But sometimes two versions of an event occupy the same position.”
Javis remembered the doubled tablet on the pavement.
“They belong to an organization called the Continuum.”
“Which version of reality gets to remain real.”
“So the photographs may be records of events that no longer exist?”
Kaelen hesitated. “Possibly someone who remembers one of them.”

scenes.label: 15 / THE SEVENTEENTH ATTEMPT
scenes.title: The Seventeenth Attempt
text: Kaelen connected a small device to a monitor. Encrypted files flickered into view.
“Fragments of Continuum records,” he said. “Incomplete. Not always reliable.”
“Someone who used to work for them.”

text.terminal:
SUBJECT DESIGNATION: J-17
STATUS: UNRESOLVED
CONTINUITY VARIANCE: CRITICAL

ITERATION 014: FAILED
ITERATION 015: FAILED
ITERATION 016: FAILED
ITERATION 017: PENDING

text: Javis checked his phone. 1:38 AM. Thirty-six minutes until the time on his death certificate.
“That depends on what they were trying to change.”
Kaelen attempted to open the next record.
The tablet warmed beneath Javis’s hand.

text.terminal:
OBSERVER LINK: ACTIVE
UNREGISTERED PRESENCE: CONFIRMED
ITERATION 017: DEVIATION DETECTED

PREVIOUS ITERATIONS: TERMINATED
CURRENT ITERATION: UNRESOLVED

text: The monitor showed a photograph of the room. Javis and Kaelen lay motionless on the floor.
Three slow knocks sounded from the entrance corridor. Javis knew those knocks.
Kaelen reached beneath his jacket. “Stay behind me.”
Javis studied the photograph. The emergency exit stood open in the image, but it was closed in the room.
“They’re showing us the wrong thing,” he said.
“The photograph isn’t warning us that we’re going to die. It’s telling us where they expect us to be.”
“Javis,” said a familiar voice from beyond the door. Professor Thorne.

text.terminal:
EXTERNAL OBSERVER: INTERVENTION DETECTED
PREDICTED OUTCOME: INVALID

text: The photograph changed. The room was empty except for a man with Javis’s face, holding the Codex and smiling.
“Please don’t make the same mistake twice,” Thorne called.
Javis looked at the other man’s left hand. There was no cut across his palm.
He opened his own hand. The thin cut was still there.
He remembered the voice behind the archive door: Because I remember getting it.
Two versions. Two different details. Perhaps two different intentions.
Not everyone wearing his face was necessarily on his side.
Somewhere inside the room, a voice whispered:

text.reveal: DON’T TRUST THE ONE WHO REMEMBERS.

scenes.label: 16 / FOUR MINUTES
scenes.title: The Room Without Records
text: The voice had come from inside the room.
Kaelen stood beside the desk, watching the monitor.
Javis looked back at the screen.
A moment earlier, it had shown two bodies on the floor of the records office. His own. Kaelen’s. Both dead.
Another Javis had appeared in their place.
The cut across his left palm was missing.
Now the monitor displayed nothing but its own dark reflection.
From beyond the entrance, Professor Thorne spoke.

text.terminal:
01:38 AM.
Four minutes until the photograph's predicted death.

text: Kaelen reached beneath his jacket and withdrew a narrow metal rod.
Kaelen looked toward the entrance. “Maybe they caught us before we reached it.”
Javis looked at the dark monitor.
Its reflection showed the rear of the room.
Kaelen followed his gaze. His face changed.
Javis scanned the room. His eyes settled on a small black disc beneath the nearest table.
Javis felt the air thicken. His knees buckled.
Kaelen lunged forward and struck the disc with his metal rod.
White light erupted. The pressure vanished.
Kaelen staggered backward, blood spilling from his nose.
Kaelen seized his sleeve and pulled him toward the emergency stairwell.
Javis pointed beneath the shelving unit.
Kaelen crossed the room, tore it open, and dropped to his knees.
Behind them, the entrance door opened.
A violent impact shook the shaft. Metal screamed somewhere behind them.
He waited for something to happen. Nothing did.
He was alive. Kaelen was alive.
Kaelen pushed past him toward a grille at the far end of the shaft.

scenes.label: 17 / THE PRICE OF ESCAPE
scenes.title: Anchors and Debts
text: The shaft ended above an abandoned loading bay.
Kaelen kicked loose the grille and lowered himself onto a stack of wooden crates.
Javis followed. His shoulder protested when he landed.
Kaelen caught his arm. “Can you move it?”
They crossed the loading bay and emerged onto a narrow street behind the records office.
Javis looked back. No smoke. No flames.
“Because running makes us easier to notice.”
Kaelen wiped blood from beneath his nose.
The metal rod in his hand had gone dull. A crack ran along its length.
Kaelen almost smiled. “An anchor forces a small area of reality to remain stable. The device I used disrupts that stabilization.”
Kaelen glanced at the broken rod. “Expensive.”
Kaelen’s expression changed. “The device doesn’t distinguish between the field it’s disrupting and the person holding it.”
Javis looked at him. “So you could have died.”
They reached a junction. Kaelen stopped beneath a broken streetlight.
Javis looked at him. “The man whose name keeps appearing in all this?”
“Why didn’t you take me there first?”
“Because I didn’t want to involve her.”
Kaelen nodded. “She left this behind years ago.”
“The Continuum. The work. All of it.”
Javis glanced back toward the records office. “And you’re going to involve her now?”
Kaelen looked at the Codex beneath Javis’s jacket. “I don’t think we have another choice.”
They turned into a narrower street.
Then Javis asked: “Are they tracking the tablet?”
“I think they may be tracking something connected to it.”
“Then why am I still carrying it?”
For the first time since they’d met, he looked genuinely uncertain.
“Because every time you’ve been separated from it,” he said, “it seems to find its way back.”
Javis thought of the alley. The tablet returning to his jacket. The impossible doorway.
“Because we don’t know what happens when it comes back.”

scenes.label: 18 / THE THREAD
scenes.title: The Workshop
text: They reached the workshop at 1:56 AM.
A faded sign hung above its shuttered entrance.
Kaelen knocked three times. Waited. Then twice more.
A small light appeared behind the frosted glass.
A woman’s voice called from inside. “Shop’s closed.”
A lock turned. The door opened a few inches.
An elderly woman looked out. Her grey hair was tied beneath a dark scarf.
She saw Kaelen’s bloodied face. Then Javis.
Kaelen leaned closer. “He has the Codex.”
For several seconds, she didn’t move.
Then she opened the door. “Inside. Both of you.”
The workshop smelled of machine oil, old wood, and dust.
Broken radios. Clock mechanisms. Disassembled engines.
A bicycle frame hung from the ceiling.
Mara locked the door behind them. Then turned to Kaelen.
Kaelen glanced at Javis. “He found it.”
Mara looked at him again. “What’s your name?”
Her expression shifted. Only slightly. But he noticed.
Mara took a slow breath. “Show me your hands.”
Her gaze settled on the fresh cut across his left hand.
She looked toward the door. “Did anyone follow you?”
Kaelen lowered his voice. “Thorne found the records office.”
She closed her eyes. For a moment, she looked very tired.
Then she pointed toward a chair. “Sit down.”
Javis remained standing. “Do you know him?”
“Then you know why he’s hunting me?”
“I know enough to be afraid that he is.”
Kaelen stepped between them. “Mara, we need information. Anything you remember about Haziah’s work. The Codex. The old records.”
Mara looked at him. “You brought him here for answers?”
“And you think answers will keep him alive?”
Mara turned away. “Answers are what got the others killed.”
Javis looked at the clock on the wall.

text.terminal:
02:00 AM.
Fourteen minutes until the predicted termination.

text: “I don’t need you to tell me everything. I need to know whether there’s something I can do before two fourteen.”
Mara slowly faced him. “Why that time?”
Javis removed his phone. He opened the photograph of Case 0017. The death report.
Mara studied the screen. Her expression changed.
She looked at Kaelen. He shook his head. “He found it himself.”
Mara read the report again. Then whispered: “They’ve started again.”
Javis stepped closer. “What does that mean?”
Mara didn’t answer. Instead, she looked at his injured shoulder. Then at the blood beneath Kaelen’s nose.
Mara exhaled. “Then you’re running out of time.”

scenes.label: 19 / THE WEAVER’S LESSON
scenes.title: The First Weave
text: Mara crossed to the workbench and lifted a damaged clock mechanism.
Several gears lay loose inside its casing.
“We don’t have time for a lesson.”
Javis looked between them. “Show me what?”
Mara placed the clock on the table. “What you’ve already been doing without understanding.”
Kaelen picked up a loose gear.
Javis examined the clock. “Broken teeth. Bent second hand. The mainspring looks damaged.”
Kaelen set down the gear. “What if the replacement parts already existed?”
Mara watched silently from beside the workbench.
Kaelen continued. “Most people see the world as a collection of fixed objects. A clock is broken or repaired. A door is open or closed.”
He placed the gear beside the mechanism.
“Every object exists within a range of possible states. A Weaver can sometimes influence which state becomes real.”
Javis stared. “That’s what happened in the alley?”
“Because I’m not going to pretend I understand everything you’ve done.”
Javis looked at the clock. “Show me.”
Kaelen placed two fingers against the mechanism.
It rose from the table. Turned.
The second hand moved. Once. Twice. Three times.
Kaelen opened his eyes. Blood appeared beneath his nose.
Kaelen lifted the mechanism. The gear slipped free and fell onto the table.
“I persuaded it to occupy a state in which it could function.”
Mara spoke from behind them. “The world doesn’t always accept being told it could have been something else.”
Javis looked at her. “That’s a strange way to describe physics.”
Mara almost smiled. “It’s a strange kind of physics.”
Javis looked at the clock. “Let me try.”
Javis examined the mechanism. The bent shaft. The damaged spring.
He placed one finger beside the gear.
Not the gear. His perception of it.
He could see the metal resting on the table.
But he could also sense another arrangement.
The same gear seated inside the clock. Turning. Connected.
“You’ve identified a possible state. That’s enough for now.”
Kaelen reached out and turned the clock over.
Inside sat a small brass wheel. Perfectly fitted. Undamaged.
Kaelen looked at Mara. She said nothing.
Javis leaned forward. “I didn’t put that there.”
On its underside was a manufacturer’s mark. A company Javis had never heard of.
Kaelen looked at her. “You recognize it?”
She nodded. “That company closed forty years ago.”
Mara looked at him. “They never manufactured clock parts.”
Kaelen turned the wheel over. Its markings were precise. Deliberate.
Javis looked at the clock. “What did I do?”
Kaelen set down the wheel. “I don’t know.”
Javis felt cold. “You said Weaving changes possibilities.”
“Then I brought something here from another possibility.”
Mara spoke quietly. “Or something found a way through while you were holding the connection open.”
Javis looked at her. The room suddenly felt smaller.

scenes.label: 20 / THE WOMAN WHO REMEMBERED
scenes.title: The Memory Spindle
text: Mara locked the brass wheel inside a small metal drawer.
Then she turned to Javis. “I need to ask you something.”
“When you were younger, did your mother ever tell you not to look at yourself in certain mirrors?”
A kitchen. Morning sunlight. His mother standing beside a sink. A mirror hanging near the doorway.
Then the image dissolved. “I don’t know.”
A woman’s voice. Gentle. Almost amused.
He opened his eyes. “She used to say something.”
Mara gripped the edge of the workbench.
Javis felt his throat tighten. “Then tell me about her.”
“There’s something you need to see first.”
She crossed to a cabinet. Kaelen followed. “Mara, are you sure?”
She opened the cabinet and removed a narrow metal cylinder.
Its surface was covered in fine markings.
Mara looked at him. “Something your mother wanted preserved.”
Javis reached for it. Mara pulled it away.
“Because you need to understand what you’re looking at.”
She placed the cylinder on the table.
“This isn’t an ordinary recording. It contains a preserved memory state.”
“Meaning the memory may not belong to the person who views it.”
Mara nodded. “And it may not show events exactly as they happened.”
Javis stared. “Then how do I know it’s real?”
He looked down at the cylinder.
His mother had wanted something preserved. Something someone else might have tried to erase.
Mara’s expression softened. “Because I promised her I would.”
Javis looked up. “You were her friend?”
“She asked me to help her do something I was afraid to do.”
Mara continued. “I’ve had a long time to regret that.”
She took a small reader from beneath the workbench. Placed the spindle inside.
A pale light spread across its surface.
“I know.” She looked at Javis. “You have a choice. We can stop now.”
He thought of the death report. The sixteen photographs. His mother’s missing face.
And the voice beneath the archive. Sixteen times they have taken you from me.
He looked at the spindle. “Show me.”

scenes.label: 21 / THE MEMORY THAT WASN’T HIS
scenes.title: The Unmaking
text: The air above the reader shimmered.
A white room. A long window overlooking a city.
Two people stood beside a desk. A man. A woman.
His father. Cassius. Younger than in the photographs.
Beside him stood Elara. His mother. Her face was clear.
He knew those eyes. He hadn’t remembered them. But something inside him recognized them immediately.
At first, the recording had no sound. Mara adjusted the reader.
Cassius stood beside the window. “We don’t have a choice.”
“No.” She turned toward him. “If we hand him over, they’ll do it again.”
Cassius looked toward the door. “Haziah says the transfer is ready.”
Cassius crossed the room. He took Elara’s hands.
“Listen to me. If they find us, you take Javis and go.”
Professor Thorne. Younger. Dark-haired. Wearing a grey uniform.
He looked nothing like the gentle professor Javis had known.
Cassius stepped between him and Elara. “You promised us safe passage.”
Thorne’s expression was unreadable. “I promised to prevent a catastrophe.”
Elara pulled away from Cassius. “You knew.”
“You knew what they were going to do to him.”
For an instant, Javis saw another room. A narrow corridor. A child crying. A door opening onto darkness.
Elara stood alone. Her face was wet with tears.
She looked directly toward the recording. Toward Javis.
As though she could see him.
“If you ever see this, remember one thing.”
A burst of static swallowed her words.
Kaelen grabbed the frame. “Mara, shut it down!”
The image twisted. Elara’s face blurred.
For one instant, the woman’s features returned. Her eyes met his.
He looked at the broken reader. At the fragments of metal. At the place where his mother’s face had been.
For the first time that night, he didn’t ask another question.
His mother’s face remained in his mind. Not perfectly. But enough.
He closed his eyes. The image remained.
He opened them again. He was afraid that if he kept them closed too long, the memory would disappear.
Kaelen gathered the fragments of the spindle. Mara stood beside the table. Neither spoke.
Javis looked at the wall clock. The second hand moved. Forty seconds.
Mara glanced at the phone. Her expression tightened.
Kaelen moved toward the door. “We need to leave.”
Javis looked at the Codex. “That’s what we’ve been doing all night.”
“Because people are trying to kill you.”
Javis looked toward the shattered spindle.
His mother had wanted him to remember something. Something important enough to preserve. Something the Continuum had tried to erase.
Javis felt something tear through him.
For one terrible instant, he couldn’t remember his own name.
He tried to speak. Nothing came.
He looked at Kaelen. Recognized his face. But couldn’t remember why.
He looked at Mara. A stranger.
His name. The archive. Thorne. The Codex. His mother.
Javis gasped. The workshop came back into focus.
Javis looked down at the tablet.

text.terminal:
SUBJECT IDENTITY: RETIRED
ACTIVE IDENTITY: UNREGISTERED

text: Mara’s face had gone pale. “They removed the identity attached to the prediction.”
Javis looked at his phone. The case file had vanished.
He searched for his university identification.
His photographs remained. But every image containing his face had changed.
He was standing in the pictures. But beneath them, the names were wrong. Dates were wrong. Locations were wrong.
Javis looked at Mara. “Can they do this to everyone?”
He looked at Kaelen. “Do you still remember me?”

scenes.label: 22 / ANOTHER FACE
scenes.title: Another Face
text: For a moment, Javis could only stare.
The man standing before him had his face.

Not a resemblance. Not the unsettling similarity of two strangers who might have shared a father. The same narrow scar near his eyebrow. The same uneven line of his jaw. Even the slight forward tilt of his head, as though he were listening to something other people couldn’t hear.
The man’s hair was shorter. His clothes were worn, particularly around the cuffs. And there was something in his expression that Javis had never seen in a mirror.
The man glanced at the floor between them.

Behind him, Mara’s workshop hummed with the quiet persistence of old machinery. The brass wheel he’d brought into existence sat on the workbench, surrounded by tools that hadn’t moved since the demonstration.
Beside it lay the black tablet.
Neither seemed particularly pleased to see the newcomer.
“No. I know what you look like.”
Javis immediately stepped into his path.
For several seconds, they regarded each other.
Then the stranger said, “Your left hand.”
That was reason enough to do it.
A thin line ran across his palm.
The skin wasn’t broken. There was no blood. The line was pale, almost silver, and it extended from the base of his thumb toward his wrist.
Mara made a quiet sound behind him.
“Would someone like to explain why everybody keeps having conversations about me as though I’m not standing here?”
“Because, Javis, most of the people who know what you are have spent a very long time trying to make sure you aren’t.”
The man considered him for a moment.
“You still give orders like you expect them to matter.”
He noticed that Kaelen hadn’t asked who the stranger was.
He noticed that Mara was looking at the man’s hands rather than his face.
Of something he expected to happen.

scenes.label: 23 / THE COST OF A SMALL THING
scenes.title: The Cost of a Small Thing
text: Mara cleared a space on the workbench.
“Before anyone says another word,” she said, “I want to see his hand.”
“Because I’d rather find out what happened to you before it happens again.”
She held out her own hand.
After a moment, he offered his.
Mara examined the pale line with a magnifying lens. She turned his wrist, pressed two fingers against his pulse, and brought a small instrument close to the mark.
“I’ve had enough interesting for one night.”
She crossed to the workbench and lifted the brass wheel.
“No,” Mara said. “I watched you bring it here.”
Mara placed the wheel beside a smaller, rusted mechanism.
The two wheels were nearly identical.
Even the same small imperfection along the outer edge.
But the rusted wheel was missing a tooth.
“I had this broken wheel for twelve years,” Mara said. “It belonged to a clock my father repaired. I kept it because I never found a replacement.”
She turned the brass wheel over.
Something in her voice made him look up.
“I didn’t ask you to repair the wheel. I asked you to imagine one that wasn’t broken.”
“And somewhere, there may have been a clock that needed this.”
He remembered the sensation of reaching toward something that wasn’t there.
“I know what you did. I don’t know where it came from.”
“Then how do you know I took it?”
“Because Weaving doesn’t create something from nothing.”
Javis looked again at the wheel.
Somewhere, perhaps, an old clock had stopped.
Perhaps someone would open it tomorrow and find an empty space.
Or perhaps it had been sitting in a box, forgotten for decades.
“That line on my hand,” he said. “That’s the price?”
“That’s evidence of an exchange. The price is something else.”
“That depends on what was taken, what replaced it, and what the exchange disturbed.”
“Every transfer has consequences,” she said. “The Continuum claims it can account for them.”
“An institution can measure a loss without understanding what it means to the person who suffered it.”

scenes.label: 24 / THE QUESTION NOBODY ANSWERED
scenes.title: The Question Nobody Answered
text: Javis sat on the edge of a low wooden stool.
His phone lay in his hand.
Five minutes past the time printed on his death certificate.

text.terminal:
SUBJECT: JAVIS
CAUSE OF DEATH: DIMENSIONAL DISPLACEMENT
DATE OF TERMINATION: 17 OCTOBER — 02:14 AM

text: He enlarged the image until the letters blurred.
“Five minutes ago,” he continued, “according to a document that apparently knows things before they happen, I was supposed to die.”
“I’m sitting here. I’m breathing. My heart’s beating. So either that document is wrong, or something happened that none of you wants to explain.”
“Not exactly. Killing someone leaves a death behind. A body. People who remember them. Records of their life.”
“A correction tries to change the history that made those things possible.”
“Because whoever issued that document considered the result equivalent.”
Javis noticed but kept his eyes on the stranger.
“And what mistake am I supposed to be?”
“No. I know what they’ve attempted. I know what happened afterward. I don’t know everything that happened before you were born.”
It was the first answer he’d received that sounded less like a riddle than an admission.
The stranger looked toward the black tablet.
“Your history began with something the Continuum considers an unresolved exchange.”
“I don’t know enough to give you a truthful answer.”
“Then why not say that in the first place?”
“Because I’ve spent too long being afraid of what happens when you know.”
“You walked in here wearing my face. You know things about me that I don’t. And everybody keeps telling me half of something and expecting me to be grateful.”
“I found a certificate saying I was going to die. A man I trusted tried to take something from me. Time stopped. I saw people who shouldn’t exist. I heard my mother’s voice.”
“And now you’re telling me somebody thinks I shouldn’t have been born.”
“I know something about what happened to her.”
“I don’t know where she is now.”
The answers hurt more than the evasions.
Because this time, he believed them.
“I don’t know what she was told before she left.”
The stranger seemed to realize what he’d revealed.
Then, very quietly, he said, “I’m sorry.”

scenes.label: 25 / SIXTEEN
scenes.title: Sixteen
text: The stranger stepped away from Javis.
“The correction hasn’t finished,” the stranger said.
Then the clock above Mara’s workbench stopped ticking.
A second later, its hands moved backward.
A narrow line of white text appeared across its surface.

text.terminal:
ORIGIN: UNRESOLVED
CORRECTION RECORDS: 017
OUTSTANDING BALANCE: UNKNOWN

text: The stranger stared at the tablet.
“I don’t know. It isn’t connected to any of my equipment.”

“Each attempt removed some part of your history. Sometimes nearly all of it. But the changes didn’t hold. Events began to produce contradictions. Records resurfaced. People remembered things they shouldn’t have remembered.”
“Then how do you know it happened?”
The stranger looked at the tablet.
Instead of numbers, there were images.
A photograph of three people standing beside a window.
The face of the person in the middle was missing.
A woman calling a name he couldn’t hear.
“Because I don’t know what accessing those records will do while a correction is active.”
The stranger looked at him for a long moment.
He thought of his friends at the university.
Of people who knew which coffee he drank and how late he stayed in the archive.
Of the small, ordinary evidence that he belonged somewhere.
It was a meaningless gesture. Something his body did because he couldn’t think of anything else.
For the first time that night, he felt something worse than fear.
He imagined a world in which nobody remembered that he’d ever been there.
And then he wondered whether such a world had already existed.

scenes.label: 26 / THE WRONG MEMORY
scenes.title: The Wrong Memory
text: Somewhere behind the walls, an old machine continued its uneven mechanical whine.
Javis wanted to believe the stranger was lying.
He wanted to believe Mara and Kaelen had arranged some elaborate deception.
And it had shown him things nobody in the room seemed prepared to explain.
“Then why do you look like me?”
“Because your identity is the one the correction is searching for.”
“It means I borrowed an appearance the system would recognize. I hoped it would give me enough time to reach you.”
“Because I couldn’t approach you under my own identity without being detected.”
The stranger glanced at the tablet.
For once, the refusal had a reason.
The stranger reached inside his coat and withdrew a small, battered notebook.
Its pages were filled with handwriting.
Some passages had been crossed out so heavily that the paper had torn.
“My attempt to remember what the Codex already knows.”
At the top of one page was a number.
The archive again. Same question. Different answer.
“Why do you keep writing the same things?”
“Because I don’t always remember writing them.”
“Then how can you be sure they’re true?”
“I can’t. That’s why I started recording details I could verify independently.”
“Dates. Locations. Objects that survived. Things that shouldn’t exist.”
“Then why should I believe anything you tell me now?”
He opened the notebook to its first page.
Do not trust the version of events that makes everything simple.
Something about the handwriting troubled him.
The way the writer crossed his sevens.
And remembered a woman sitting beside a window.
She was writing in a small notebook.
A child was laughing somewhere nearby.
Javis could not see the child’s face.
Then he whispered something Javis couldn’t hear.
“But I think you just remembered something that doesn’t belong to the history you’ve lived.”
“Don’t assume every memory is a memory of what happened here.”
“It means an event can have more than one possible history.”
“And sometimes, when those histories touch, something crosses over.”
Javis thought of the woman by the window.
Of the child laughing somewhere he couldn’t see.
And of the notebook in his hands.
For once, Javis didn’t press him.
He was beginning to understand that not knowing could be more frightening than a lie.

scenes.label: 27 / THE PRICE OF STAYING
scenes.title: The Price of Staying
text: One after another, beginning at the far end of the workshop.
A row of darkness moved toward them.
Mara seized a lamp from beneath the workbench.
It wasn’t simply the absence of light.
Simply ceasing to occupy the space where they had stood.
The black tablet vibrated against the workbench.
The stranger pulled him toward the rear of the workshop.
“If this has happened sixteen times, why are you all acting like we can run from it?”
Tools struck the floor where its surface had been.
“Because,” the stranger said, “this time you know.”
“And knowing changes what you can choose.”
For a moment, they stood facing each other.
Then he held out the notebook.
The man pressed it into his hands.
As though someone had left it beside a fire.
“Listen,” the stranger said. “The next time someone tells you your existence is a mistake, ask them who made the mistake.”
There was no flash of light.
His features simply began to lose their certainty.
The scar near his eyebrow faded.
For a heartbeat, Javis saw an unfamiliar face beneath his own.
But before he could answer, the darkness reached him.
Only a sharp intake of breath.
The stranger looked toward the Codex.
For a moment, something like hope crossed his face.
The tablet remained on the workbench.
Putting something back doesn’t mean everything that happened while it was missing can be undone.
An object could cross from one reality into another.
An exchange could preserve something that otherwise wouldn’t remain.
But nothing came without a consequence.
The notebook might disappear with him.
And if it did, Javis would lose the only personal record of what had happened before.
“Javis, we don’t know what it will cost.”
The man’s face was almost gone.
Javis held the notebook against the black tablet.
He remembered the sensation of reaching for the brass wheel.
This time, he didn’t reach for something absent.
He reached for something already there.
The notebook grew hot beneath his fingers.
The silver line returned to his palm.
Javis felt a sudden pressure behind his eyes.
For an instant, he saw two workshops occupying the same space.
Only a bare room with a window overlooking a street he didn’t recognize.
The notebook remained in his hands.
Even the tools were back in their places.
Javis stood in the middle of the room, clutching the notebook.
Kaelen stared at the empty space where the stranger had stood.
Javis looked down at his hand.
Where the stranger’s handwriting had ended, a new sentence had appeared.
Then looked toward the workshop clock.
His phone had shown 02:19 only minutes earlier.
Now every clock in the room displayed the same time.
Behind them, the black tablet illuminated one final time.
Then, from somewhere beyond the workshop door, came the sound of footsteps.
A familiar voice spoke from the other side.
He had heard it in a memory that wasn’t his.
He had heard it in the recording from the spindle.
The notebook slipped slightly in his hands.

scenes.label: 28 / THE VOICE BEHIND THE DOOR
scenes.title: The Voice Behind the Door
text: For years, he’d imagined hearing his mother’s voice again.
Sometimes in dreams. Sometimes in the moments between waking and sleep, when the mind was cruel enough to make an absence feel temporary.
He’d imagined what she might say.
He had never imagined she would tell him to stay away.
His voice sounded smaller than he intended.
A pause. Then: “I need you to listen carefully.”
It was her voice. Not merely the same pitch or accent. There was a particular softness at the end of her sentences, a habit of speaking as though she were sharing a secret.
He remembered it. Or thought he did.
A faint sound came from the other side. It might have been a laugh.
“You used to ask me that when I came home late.”
“You’d hide behind the kitchen door,” the voice continued. “And make me prove I wasn’t a stranger.”
He remembered. A small kitchen. Yellow curtains. His mother’s shopping bags on the floor. A boy trying not to laugh.
“I’d tell you something only your mother knew.”
Javis closed his eyes. “And what was that?”
Then the voice answered. “You were afraid of the dark until you were nine. But you never wanted anyone to know.”
Javis opened his eyes. That was true.
He hadn’t thought about it in years.
“So did the man who wore your face,” Mara replied.
Javis looked at her. The words struck harder than she’d intended.
Mara seemed to realize it. “I’m not saying it isn’t her.”
“I’m saying we don’t know what is on the other side.”
The voice spoke again. “Mara is right.”
Javis stared at the door. “You know Mara?”

For an instant, he heard his mother in those words. Not the voice. The person. The woman who had once refused to help him with a school assignment because she wanted him to learn how to solve it himself.
He felt an almost unbearable urge to open the door.
The answer came quietly. “Somewhere I shouldn’t be able to reach you.”
Kaelen approached the workshop’s security panel. A small screen beside the rear entrance displayed a grainy image of the corridor outside.
He adjusted the camera. Nothing changed.
Javis looked from the screen to the door. “Then who’s talking?”
The voice responded. “I’m not standing in your corridor.”
Mara approached the tablet. Its display still read:
She examined the screen without touching it.
“Javis,” she said, “what exactly did you do to the notebook?”
“I tried to keep it from disappearing.”
“The same way I brought the wheel here.”

“Not quite.” She pointed toward his palm. The silver line had darkened into a narrow, almost black mark. “With the wheel, you reached for something elsewhere. With the notebook, you were trying to stop something already here from leaving.”
Kaelen turned from the security panel. “Whatever he did, it happened at the same time the correction failed.”
Mara nodded. “And the voice appeared afterward.”
Javis looked at the notebook. The final sentence remained.
“What if that’s what happened? What if I reached into another reality and brought her close enough to speak?”
The voice answered before Mara could. “You didn’t bring me anywhere.”
Javis turned toward the door. “Then how are you here?”
The voice continued. “I was in my kitchen. I heard someone calling, and then I heard you. I haven’t moved.”
Javis looked at the door. “Can you see me?”
The voice hesitated. “People speaking. A clock. Someone crying.”
Mara looked sharply at the tablet. For an instant, the display flickered.
Mara glanced at the workshop clock. Its hands remained frozen at 02:14.
“Because whatever you’re hearing, we haven’t established that the space beyond it is still the corridor.”
Kaelen checked the security feed again. Still empty.
Javis turned back toward the door. “How do you know it’s me?”
When it returned, it sounded less certain. “Because you called me Mother.”
Javis felt the answer settle inside him.
He wanted it to be enough.
Then she said a name he didn’t recognize.
Javis went cold. “That isn’t my name.”
He stared at the door. “You’re not my mother.”
“I know the name I gave my son.”
“Then why do you remember my kitchen? My childhood?”
The answer was so immediate that Javis had no response.
The voice continued. “I remember the yellow curtains. I remember you hiding behind the door. I remember your father complaining that you were getting too old for those games.”
“How old is your son?” he asked.
A long silence followed. “He would be older now.”
“How old was he when you last saw him?”
He had been older than seven when his mother disappeared.
He remembered standing in the hallway while his father argued with someone behind a locked door. He remembered a suitcase. He remembered his mother kneeling to straighten his collar.
He searched for the memory. It was there, but the edges seemed uncertain. Like a photograph handled too many times.
The voice behind the door was crying. Not loudly. Just enough that he could hear her trying to control it.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “I don’t know what’s happening. I heard someone calling, and then I heard your voice.”
Javis looked at the notebook. He thought of the memory he’d seen. A woman beside a window. A child laughing somewhere nearby.
He hadn’t seen the child’s face.
“Your son,” he said carefully. “What happened to him?”

scenes.label: 29 / A DOOR THAT WASN'T THERE
scenes.title: A Door That Wasn't There
text: Javis stared at the closed door.
He waited for it to return.
He pressed his ear against the door.
There was no breathing on the other side. No movement. Nothing.
She took the notebook carefully. Her expression darkened as she examined it.
The dark line had begun to spread toward his wrist.
Mara took a small instrument from the workbench. She held it near his palm.
The instrument clicked. Then emitted a low, continuous tone.
“Javis, when you preserved the notebook, did you feel anything leave you?”
He thought about it. The pressure behind his eyes. The two workshops. The notebook existing in both.
There was something he couldn’t remember.
Something ordinary. Something that had been there a moment ago.
“What was the first thing your mother taught you to cook?” Mara asked.

He opened his mouth. He knew the answer. Of course he knew. He remembered standing beside her in the kitchen. He remembered the smell of onions. The warmth of the stove. The way she would tap his fingers away when he tried to steal food.
Mara nodded slowly. “Try something else. What colour were the kitchen curtains?”
“What did she call you when you were little?”
He knew she’d had a name for him. Something silly. Something he’d hated when he was older. He could remember being embarrassed by it.
Javis looked down at his hand. “What did I do?”
Mara didn’t answer immediately. Then she said: “I think you paid for the notebook with something you couldn’t see.”
“It’s one possibility. I can’t prove it yet.”
He laughed once. A broken sound. “That’s becoming everyone’s favourite answer.”
He had saved it. He had kept something from disappearing.
And now he couldn’t remember what his mother used to call him.
For a long time, nobody spoke.
Then Mara quietly added: “There’s something else we need to consider.”
“The notebook may not have been the only thing affected by your exchange.”
“Possibly. But I don’t know whether your action caused the connection or whether both were consequences of the correction.”
Javis looked toward the door. “Then we shouldn’t assume anything.”

scenes.label: 30 / MORNING, EVENTUALLY
scenes.title: Morning, Eventually
text: By morning, Javis had learned three things about Mara Voss.
She hated people touching her tools without permission.
She drank her tea without sugar.
And she could sleep through almost anything except the sound of someone using the wrong screwdriver.
Mara stood in the doorway, her hair tied into an untidy knot.
He glanced at the screwdriver in his hand.
“It has a handle. It has a metal end. I’m reasonably confident.”
Across the room, Kaelen laughed into his cup.
“How long have you two known each other?”
Javis noticed that Mara’s irritation seemed familiar to Kaelen.
For the first time since entering the workshop, Javis felt like he’d stepped into a place where people had lives before he arrived.
He wasn’t sure why that mattered.
The clock above the workbench read 8:43.
It had started moving again sometime before dawn.
Javis had checked his phone repeatedly throughout the night. Time had continued normally, though he no longer trusted that as proof of anything.
The black tablet remained dark beneath its glass cover.
The notebook lay beside his bedroll.
And the dark line across his palm hadn’t faded.
“Is that an invitation or a warning?”
She disappeared into the adjoining room.
From the kitchen came Mara’s voice.
For a moment, Javis almost forgot about the Continuum.
Then he looked at the photograph of his parents.
And remembered why he was there.

scenes.label: 31 / A TABLE FOR THREE
scenes.title: A Table for Three
text: Mara’s kitchen was barely large enough for its table.
A narrow window overlooked the neighbouring rooftops. Several potted herbs crowded the sill, most of them thriving despite the poor light.
Mara had left it there anyway.
“Because she’ll tell you she’s reviving it.”
“I am reviving it,” Mara said, placing three plates on the table.
Mara set a plate in front of him.
Bread. Eggs. Something that might once have been a tomato.
“And somehow still has better manners than you.”
Mara gave Kaelen a pointed look.
For several minutes, nobody mentioned corrections, death certificates, or alternate realities.
Javis discovered that Kaelen disliked eggs with runny yolks.
Mara discovered that Javis had once worked part-time repairing university equipment.
And Javis discovered that Mara’s workshop had nearly been closed twice because she refused to sell it to a development company.
“My father built most of it. I grew up here.”
“She also rejected an offer that would’ve paid for three workshops.”
“Some places are worth more than what someone will pay for them.”
Kaelen looked down at his plate.
“I was just thinking about the last time you said that.”
“A long time ago, someone offered to relocate the workshop.”
“Because the equipment couldn’t be moved without destroying half of it.”
“The Continuum wanted access to something my father had built. They offered to buy the property. When I refused, they offered to move everything.”
“A machine that could detect certain kinds of transfers.”
“Like the instrument you used on my hand?”
“Because I discovered they weren’t interested in detecting transfers.”
“They wanted to identify people who could perform them.”
“And I wasn’t going to hand them a list.”
“Every time I need a component I can no longer manufacture.”
“But I don’t regret keeping it out of their hands.”
For the first time, he understood that Mara’s workshop wasn’t simply a hiding place.
It was something she’d already fought to protect.
And his presence might put it at risk again.

scenes.label: 32 / THE PLAN
scenes.title: The Plan
text: After breakfast, Javis spread the contents of the metal case across the workbench.
A sheet of paper on which he’d written everything he could remember from the previous night.
The Continuum issued a correction order.
The photograph may contain evidence of a transfer.
My memories may have been affected by an exchange.
Cassius may have performed an unauthorized Weave.
The corrections may be connected to that event.
The voice may have come from another history.
Why is my existence considered unresolved?
What did I lose when I preserved the notebook?
“And whether the Continuum understands why the previous corrections failed.”
“You’re not walking into a Continuum facility.”
“No. You agreed you wouldn’t make decisions for me.”
“I agreed you could make your own decisions. I didn’t agree to help you get killed.”
“You know what I’m going to say.”
“Yes. That’s why I’m asking you not to.”
“Continuum records aren’t stored in one place. The central registry keeps official versions, but certain departments maintain working copies.”
“Some of those copies are transferred periodically to independent archives for verification.”
“Institutions that aren’t supposed to answer directly to the Continuum.”
Javis thought about the restricted archive.
“You’re saying the university might have more records.”
“I’m saying it may have copies of records that the Continuum believes are inaccessible.”
“We barely got him out of there.”
“And they probably expect us to stay away.”
“Then perhaps that’s exactly where we should look.”
“We don’t have to go back immediately. We need to find out what records exist and how to access them.”

scenes.label: 33 / WHAT MARA KEPT
scenes.title: What Mara Kept
text: The argument ended without a decision.
Kaelen went outside to check whether anyone had followed them.
Javis remained in the workshop, examining Mara’s collection of instruments.
He was careful not to touch anything.
Then returned to a small device she’d been repairing.
“Because newer systems are easier to monitor.”
Then he noticed a photograph pinned above the workbench.
A younger Mara stood beside an older man.
Behind them was the same workshop.
“Then why build machines to detect it?”
“Because he believed understanding something was the first step toward making it safer.”
“My father built a detector that could identify unusual transfers. He thought it would help prevent accidents.”
“They told him they wanted to fund his research. He was thrilled. He’d spent years working alone, and suddenly people with resources were interested.”
“He gave them access to his designs.”
“But you said you dismantled the machine.”
“By then, they’d already used his work.”
Mara picked up her tool again.
“That’s why I don’t accuse them of killing him.”
She wasn’t pretending to know more than she did.
“Is that why you still work on the detectors?”
“Because my father was right about one thing.”
She turned the receiver toward him.
“But only if the people doing the understanding care what happens afterward.”
“Do you know anything about signal calibration?”
“Enough to know that isn’t a screwdriver.”
Then she handed him a tool.
For the next hour, they worked.
And for the first time since the archive, Javis felt useful in a way that had nothing to do with being unusual.

scenes.label: 34 / AN OLD FRIEND
scenes.title: An Old Friend
text: A woman followed him into the workshop.
She was tall, with closely cropped hair and a long coat that had seen better days.
She carried a small canvas bag.
The woman set the bag down on the workbench.
Javis watched, aware of yet another history he didn’t know.
“Relax. I’m not here to tell you you’re special.”
“I’m here because Kaelen owes me money.”
“I promised I wouldn’t mention how much.”
For a moment, the workshop felt almost ordinary.
Then Liora placed a small storage device on the table.
“Continuum historical files are being moved between registries tomorrow night. Some are being sent to the university for verification.”
“One shipment includes material from a sealed investigation.”
“Now that,” he said, “I can help with.”

scenes.label: 35 / THE COST OF A PLAN
scenes.title: The Cost of a Plan
text: By evening, the workshop table had disappeared beneath maps, diagrams, and notes.
Liora had drawn the university’s service routes.
Mara had listed the equipment they might need.
Javis had sketched the archive’s internal layout from memory.
For once, he wasn’t the person asking all the questions.
He was the one answering them.
“The eastern corridor has two cameras,” he explained. “But one points toward the stairwell. It doesn’t cover the records entrance.”
“People rarely notice the person carrying boxes.”
“I said I worked there. I didn’t say I was a criminal.”
“The transfer happens tomorrow night. But the university will know the files are arriving.”
“Then we need a reason for the security team to be somewhere else,” Kaelen said.
“We’re not creating a distraction that puts innocent people at risk.”
“We need access without forcing our way in.”
“When new historical records arrive, someone from the university checks the shipment against its catalogue.”
“And they sometimes call in temporary staff when there’s a backlog.”
“Not under my own name. Not after what happened.”
“I’ve heard enough plans that begin with everyone looking at me.”
Javis pointed toward the archive entrance.
“We don’t need to steal the shipment. We need to know which records are in it.”
“If we can get a copy of the verification catalogue, we can identify the files we need without opening the sealed containers.”
“Then we can decide whether the actual records are worth the risk.”
“And how do we get the catalogue?”
“That’s the part we still need to solve.”
For the first time, he felt something resembling control.
But because he had people around him who could do things he couldn’t.
And because, this time, he was helping decide what happened next.

scenes.label: 36 / THE MESSAGE
scenes.title: The Message
text: The receiver crackled just after sunset.
Mara was alone at the workbench when the signal arrived.
She glanced toward the adjoining room.
Javis and Liora were still arguing about the archive’s service entrance.
Kaelen was outside checking the street.
Her hand tightened around the receiver.
“He called his first detector the Nightingale.”
Nobody outside the workshop had known that name.
Her father had chosen it because the machine produced a high, wavering tone whenever it detected an unstable transfer.
He’d joked that it sang whenever reality was out of tune.
The Continuum had renamed the device when they acquired his research.
The Nightingale had never appeared in the official documentation.
“Where did you hear that name?” Mara demanded.
“Your father discovered a flaw in the Nightingale’s readings. He documented it in a supplementary report.”
“Because the flaw wasn’t in the machine.”
“It was in what they were using it to measure.”
She glanced toward the adjoining room.
Javis was bent over a map, listening while Liora explained something.
“Ask yourself why a detector designed to identify unstable transfers was eventually used to identify people.”
She had asked herself that question for years.
“The final page contains a handwritten correction. Your father crossed out the word origin and replaced it with consequence.”
Mara stopped breathing for a moment.
Her father had argued about it constantly during the final months of his research.
A machine could detect the disturbance left by an exchange, he’d said, but that didn’t mean it could identify the person responsible.
“Station Nine. The old industrial district. Tomorrow, before midnight.”
She had visited the station with her father once.
“Because someone in your workshop is already connected to the investigation.”
Mara’s fingers tightened around the receiver.
“Your father tried to correct the record.”
She looked toward the adjoining room.
Javis was laughing at something Liora had said.
They were preparing to risk their lives searching for records that might explain Javis’s existence.
And now Mara had been offered something she had wanted for years.
Kaelen would insist on accompanying her.
Javis would ask questions she wasn’t ready to answer.
Liora would probably tell her the meeting was a trap.
Mara reached for a piece of paper.
Then she folded the note and slipped it into her coat.
She looked at the receiver again.
Her father had once told her that a good scientist should never fall in love with an explanation.
Mara had spent years believing she understood why his work had been taken.
From the adjoining room, Kaelen called:
She had spent the morning criticizing Kaelen for keeping things from Javis.
Now she was keeping something from all of them.
That didn’t make telling them any easier.

scenes.label: 37 / THE MORNING AFTER
scenes.title: The Morning After
text: Javis woke to the smell of burning bread.
For a moment, he thought he was home.
There was a kitchen somewhere beyond the room. Someone was moving plates. A man was complaining about breakfast.
He lay on a narrow couch beneath a blanket that smelled faintly of machine oil.
Across the room, Kaelen stood beside the stove.
“Kaelen, that bread has crossed into another state of matter.”
“Oh, good. He’s awake. Tell her this is edible.”
Kaelen set the pan down with exaggerated dignity.
“Fine. No breakfast for any of you.”
“You’re the one who burned it,” Mara said.
Kaelen glanced toward the workshop’s rear window.
He also noticed that Kaelen didn’t look at him.
Kaelen turned back to the stove.
She picked up a small instrument.
For a moment, the workshop felt almost ordinary again.
Then Liora came in from the back room, holding a tablet.
She placed the tablet on the table.
“Because her department is receiving a shipment tomorrow night. And because I think I know how to get inside the verification office without breaking in.”
He had the sudden, uncomfortable feeling that this conversation had already been decided before he entered the room.
Kaelen was still facing the stove.
For a moment, his expression was unreadable.

scenes.label: 38 / A DIFFERENT WAY IN
scenes.title: A Different Way In
text: “An anonymous transmission. On the old receiver.”
“It asked her to come to Station Nine. Alone.”
“The caller claimed to have a report the Continuum suppressed. He said my father tried to correct a record, and someone stopped him.”
Kaelen moved away from the stove.
“I was going to think about it.”
Kaelen stopped a few feet from her.
“That’s not what people do when they’re thinking about it.”
“Turn this into a lecture about trust.”
“Yes, it is. That’s what it always is with you.”
“Mara, you should have told us. I understand why you didn’t. Both of those things can be true.”
“And Kaelen, if someone in this room received a message about their family, I think you’d want to know before they acted on it.”
“I’m not asking you to apologize. I’m asking you to stop treating every decision as though you’re the only one who can make it.”
“Now tell me about the verification office.”
“The University Historical Verification Office processes incoming Continuum shipments before they reach the archive. The officer who signs off on the manifest is Dr. Selene Ardent.”
“The same Ardent whose signature was on the altered shipment notice?”
Javis sat down at the table.
“Then we can’t just use her card.”
“No. But we can go to her office as researchers requesting catalogue access.”
“The one the office was built for. A researcher can request to verify a historical record against the catalogue.”
“No. But it would give us the shipment reference number. And if the reference number matches the one in our evidence, we’d have official confirmation that the shipment exists.”
“And if we want the actual manifest?”
“You don’t even know what she’s going to say.”
“She’s going to suggest we send someone in under a false identity.”
“Because I know how to walk into an institutional building without anyone remembering I was there.”
Then he looked back at Liora.
“We’re not sending anyone in. Not yet.”
“She signed a document she didn’t approve. She knows something is wrong. She’s already a potential ally. We’re not going to get a better one.”
“We’re going to approach her publicly. Somewhere she can’t quietly disappear us. And we’re going to ask her what she knows about the shipment.”
“Don’t start agreeing with him just because we argued.”
“I’m agreeing with him because he’s right.”
“If this goes wrong, we don’t make decisions for each other. We make them together.”
“Then let’s find out who Dr. Ardent is.”

scenes.label: 39 / THE WOMAN IN THE CATALOGUE
scenes.title: The Woman in the Catalogue
text: Dr. Selene Ardent was shorter than Javis remembered.
She stood at the front of the verification hearing room, adjusting papers with quick, precise movements.
Two administrative staff sat behind a desk at the back. A single other observer, an older man with a worn briefcase, sat in the last row.
Javis and Liora entered the room a few minutes before the session began.
“No weapons,” he’d said. “No recording devices. We’re asking questions, not picking a fight.”
Mara had stayed at the workshop, monitoring the receiver.
Javis watched Ardent set down her papers.
Her gaze moved across the room.
For a moment, her expression didn’t change.
Then she looked down at her papers again.
Two routine verifications. A disputed archival date. A classification disagreement.
When it ended, Javis and Liora waited until the other observer left.
“I worked in the university archive. In the period before the restricted collections were sealed.”
“We’re investigating a historical transfer record. We believe it was altered.”
“Submit an inquiry through the verification office.”
Javis pulled a folded sheet of paper from his jacket.
He placed it on the desk in front of her.
“This is the altered shipment notice. It bears your signature.”
Ardent looked down at the paper.
Ardent was silent for a moment.
Then she picked up the paper and examined it more closely.
“When did you say you found this?”
“And what did you do when you found it?”
“I read it. I tried to find out what it meant.”
“Mr. Javis, if that is your real name, you should know that any investigation into a classified shipment requires a formal request through the Continuum’s reconciliation division.”
Ardent looked at him for a long moment.
“It means the document was created using an authorization I issued for a different shipment. The signature is mine. The approval is not.”
She looked toward the administrative staff at the back of the room.
“I’d like to continue this conversation somewhere more private.”
Ardent led them to a small office at the end of the corridor.
“I don’t know who changed the shipment notice. But I know it was changed.”
“Because the original approval exists. It was issued for a transfer to the Central Repository. Someone amended the destination without reauthorizing the shipment.”
Javis looked at the paper in her hand.
“The system doesn’t distinguish between the original approval and a copied reference. Anyone with access to the authorization file could reuse the signature.”
“The verification office. Continuum reconciliation staff. Anyone who has been granted temporary administrative authority.”
Then he asked the question that had been forming since he entered the room.
“Do you know what was in the shipment?”
“A sealed investigation. That’s all I was told.”
“And the destination was changed to Annex C?”
He opened the shipment notice he had photographed in the archive.
“Do you know anyone who could have done this without your knowledge?”
“I’d like to see the original approval.”
“If the original approval still exists, it may list the shipment’s authorized destination. That could tell us whether the change was made before or after the shipment left the Continuum.”
“The original approval is stored with the shipment record. That record is held in a Continuum-controlled archive.”
Ardent was silent for a moment.
“I can request it. But the request will be logged.”
“Then maybe we should think about this differently.”
“Instead of requesting the record, maybe we should ask why the shipment was ever sent to Annex C in the first place.”
“And how do you propose to do that?”
Javis placed the shipment notice on her desk.
“By watching the next shipment to Annex C. And by finding out who receives it.”
Ardent was silent for a long moment.
Then she picked up the shipment notice and held it between them.
“No,” Javis said. “I’m just very tired of being lied to.”
Ardent studied him for a moment longer.
Then she set the notice down.
“There’s something else. The original approval for the shipment to the Central Repository — it was issued three days before the notice was created.”
“It suggests the destination was changed after the approval.”
Javis looked at the notice again.
“Do you know who authorized the change?” he asked.
“The change would require a separate approval. If the approval was logged, we could find it. If it wasn’t—”
“Then someone made the change without permission.”

“I should tell you,” she said, “that if the shipment record contains evidence of unauthorized modification, the Continuum will treat the record as classified and restrict access to it. You may not be able to view it.”
Javis glanced at the shipment notice.
“Someone who was at the gate when the van arrived.”
“A security officer will not speak to you if they believe the Continuum is watching. And after last night, the Continuum will be watching.”
He had no answer to that.

scenes.label: 40 / AN UNFINISHED DEBT
scenes.title: An Unfinished Debt
text: Liora found Kaelen outside the workshop an hour later.
He stood beneath the narrow awning, watching rainwater drip from the gutter.
“Pretending you’re thinking when you’re actually worrying.”
“Years ago, the Continuum used university facilities for temporary holding.”
