“Witnesses. Researchers. Anyone connected to an investigation who couldn’t be moved openly.”
“That’s the problem with you, Kaelen. You always know when something was wrong. Just usually afterward.”
“I didn’t come here to judge you.”
“Because she wanted someone who could move records without asking too many questions.”
“She also asked whether I knew anything about Station Nine.”
He stared at the workshop door.
“Nothing good ever came out of Station Nine.”

scenes.label: 41 / THE CHOICE
scenes.title: The Choice
text: Javis was reviewing the altered shipment notice when Kaelen returned.
She was working at the far bench.
People deciding what he needed to know.
“If something affects the investigation, tell me.”
“Have you been asking about Station Nine?”
She took out the folded paper.
“They claimed to have information about my father’s research.”
“I know what you’re going to say.”
“Then you know why I’m saying it.”
“Someone contacts you anonymously, claims to know something about your father, and asks you to come alone to an abandoned facility?”
He could see how easily the argument might become something else.
The distinction between origin and consequence.
When she finished, Javis was silent.
“Was the detail about your father’s report something anyone could have known?”
“Could someone have learned it from his notes?”
“Not by walking into Station Nine alone.”
Javis looked at the altered shipment notice.
Then at the location written on Mara’s paper.
“I’m suggesting we find out whether the two are connected.”
“Mara asked me a question. She didn’t ask me to report it to you.”
“Just don’t make the decision for us.”
For a moment, she said nothing.

scenes.label: 42 / THE CONNECTION
scenes.title: The Connection
text: She compared public property records, university maintenance contracts, and historical transport routes.
Javis helped identify the university’s old service corridors.
Mara supplied technical information about Station Nine.
By early evening, they had something.
Liora turned the screen toward them.
“Annex C and Station Nine were both part of the same research programme.”
“It was supposed to investigate discrepancies in official records.”
“Station Nine handled experimental equipment. Annex C stored research records and temporary evidence.”
“So Cassius’s files might pass through Annex C before being transferred elsewhere.”
A list of research equipment appeared.
Beside the entry was a date.
Three months after her father’s death.
“Prototype Three was dismantled before he died.”
“Possibly. But not without the original specifications.”
And connected to a programme investigating historical discrepancies.
For the first time, their separate questions had led to the same place.
“Which means the message may have been intended to bring you into the investigation.”
“Or someone wants me to find something.”
“Either way, we now have a reason to examine Annex C.”
“The shipment arrives at Annex C tomorrow night. Station Nine’s meeting is before midnight.”
“So if we divide our attention, we increase the risk.”
“We don’t have to go to both.”
“We go where the evidence is moving.”
For a moment, she seemed disappointed.

scenes.label: 43 / THE EMPTY ANNEX
scenes.title: The Empty Annex
text: The following evening, rain returned to the city.
Annex C stood at the edge of the university grounds, separated from the main archive by a narrow service road.
A faded sign warned of structural instability.
Javis crouched behind a low wall with Kaelen.
Across the road, Liora watched the service entrance from a parked vehicle.
Mara remained in the workshop, monitoring the receiver and the equipment she’d prepared.
They had agreed that someone needed to stay behind.
Javis suspected it had cost her more than she admitted.
The shipment was scheduled to arrive at 22:40.
They weren’t going to break into the annex.
Confirm whether the altered destination was being used.
Then decide what to do next.
Javis looked toward the dark building.
The metal gleamed faintly beneath the rain.
“But if they’re expecting a delivery, why chain the main entrance?”
Then spoke quietly into his communicator.
Javis looked at the building again.
A vehicle approached from the eastern road.
The other approached the chained entrance.
The van’s rear compartment slid upward.
One bore a familiar reference number.
The chain returned to its original position.
“That vehicle was decommissioned six years ago.”
For an instant, he saw movement behind an upper window.
“The shipment wasn’t delivered to the university.”
“It was taken somewhere the university believes is closed.”
“Then this isn’t just a records transfer.”
Javis looked back at the building.

scenes.label: 44 / THE RECORD THAT MOVED
scenes.title: The Record That Moved
text: They returned to Mara’s workshop shortly after midnight.
“Six years,” she said, pacing. “That vehicle has been listed as destroyed for six years.”
He handed her a sheet of paper.
She compared it with the transfer schedule.
Mara turned the screen toward him.
The records now showed a perfectly ordinary transfer.
Then, without anyone touching it, the screen illuminated.
Javis looked back at the screen.
Liora looked from the tablet to Javis.
“Does that mean your father is alive?”
He wanted to ask a hundred questions.
And a record could be active without the person named in it being alive.
Somewhere inside Annex C, someone had moved a record.
Someone had altered the official account.
For the first time, Javis wasn’t simply discovering that history had been changed.
He looked toward the photograph of his parents.
“Whatever they’re doing,” he said, “they’re still doing it.”
And somewhere in the city, a sealed investigation bearing his father’s name had become active again.

scenes.label: 45 / THE MORNING REPORT
scenes.title: The Morning Report
text: By eight in the morning, Javis had discovered that the Continuum could make a building disappear without moving a single brick.
Or at least, someone could make the records insist it had disappeared.
He was staring at a university maintenance notice.
The document was dated six months earlier.
Across the workbench, Liora looked up from her breakfast.
He turned the screen toward her.
“And now the university says the building was demolished six months ago.”
Liora took the terminal from him.
She searched the university’s property register.
The site was listed as vacant.
He studied the records without speaking.
“According to the system? Six months ago.”
“You think someone fabricated all this overnight?”
“I think someone wants the official record to say Annex C doesn’t exist.”
“Could it be a correction?” Javis asked.
“Possibly,” she replied. “But records can be falsified without Weaving.”
Javis looked toward the black tablet.
It sat beneath its glass cover.
He had spent much of the night waiting for it to illuminate again.
“Not unless there’s another exchange it recognizes.”
“Then we need something the university can’t quietly rewrite.”
“The one at the western service gate. He checked the road when the van arrived.”
But Liora was still looking at the screen.

scenes.label: 46 / THE MAN AT THE GATE
scenes.title: The Man at the Gate
text: Finding the guard took most of the morning.
The university’s current security roster had been removed from public access.
Liora found an older staff directory, but the photographs were outdated and several names had been reassigned.
They eventually identified three possible guards who might have worked the western gate.
“It means someone there understands basic security.”
“Could we identify the guard from the vehicle footage?”
“The camera angle doesn’t show his face clearly.”
The guard was little more than a dark figure beneath a streetlamp.
He remembered seeing the man step out of the gatehouse.
“Security officers sign the vehicle log whenever they inspect traffic near the service road.”
“The university’s transport office receives copies when there’s a delivery dispute. I used to help reconcile those records.”
“Possibly. But we’d need a legitimate reason.”
“You want to file an administrative discrepancy?”
They submitted a request through the university’s public records office.
And that frustrated him more than he wanted to admit.
They spent the next two hours examining what they already possessed.
Nothing gave them the guard’s identity.
By midday, Javis was ready to abandon the search.
Three weeks earlier, a security officer had submitted a public grievance about unpaid overtime at the western service gate.
But there was still no proof he’d worked the previous night.
“We need to ask him,” Javis said.

scenes.label: 47 / AN ORDINARY MAN
scenes.title: An Ordinary Man
text: Tomas Reed refused their first request to meet.
I don’t know you. Please contact university administration.
Then placed the terminal on the table.
“He might. But he doesn’t owe us a conversation.”

I understand. We witnessed an unusual delivery near the western service gate last night. We believe the official record may be inaccurate. If you were on duty, we would appreciate the chance to compare what we saw. If not, we won’t contact you again.
Javis tried to concentrate on the transport records.
The café was nearly empty when Reed arrived.
He was broad-shouldered, with tired eyes and a greying beard.
He wore a faded blue jacket over his security uniform.
Reed looked toward the café entrance.
The two figures entering Annex C.
When Javis finished, the older man leaned back.
Reed gave him a strange look.
“My supervisor showed it to me this morning.”
“He told me to withdraw my report.”
As though the answer should have been obvious.
“They told me I’d been confused. That I’d mistaken a construction fence for a building.”
“Did you keep a copy of your report?”
“I’ve got eleven years at that university. Eleven years without a disciplinary warning. Now they’re telling me I should see a doctor.”
“My wife thinks I should let it go.”
“I think someone is changing the records.”
“I can’t explain how. But we were there. We saw what you saw.”
He could tell Reed about Cassius.
But the man had already made it clear that he didn’t want to be drawn into something dangerous.
“Someone close to me is connected to what was delivered.”
He removed a folded piece of paper.
“My supervisor asked me to sign this.”
He placed it on the table.
The statement claimed Reed had misidentified the location and had no evidence of an unauthorized delivery.
At the bottom was a blank signature line.
For the first time, his expression softened slightly.
“Whatever you decide, you should keep your own account somewhere safe.”
“Because if the official report changes, you may want a record of what you originally said.”
“If you want someone outside the university to have a copy, you can send it to this address.”
He wrote down a contact address Liora had prepared for receiving evidence.
Then placed it beside the unsigned statement.
Javis watched him disappear into the street.
“You handled that better than I expected.”
“Sometimes giving someone information changes what they feel they can ignore.”
“I didn’t tell him what to do.”

scenes.label: 48 / THE REPORT
scenes.title: The Report
text: They returned to the workshop shortly after six.
“Reed’s supervisor wants him to withdraw his report.”
Javis placed the unsigned statement on the table.
“He let me read it. I copied the wording with his permission.”
“Because we’re not collecting evidence at the expense of the people who provide it.”
She opened the university’s incident register.
The report listed Tomas Reed as the reporting officer.
Unauthorized vehicle observed near vacant construction site.
Then noticed a line near the bottom.
Javis felt a surge of relief.
“The photograph was uploaded after our meeting.”
“University security. Administration. Any external agency with verification authority.”
Liora was already checking the available controls.
A moment later, she shook her head.
Reed had chosen to preserve evidence.
But he’d placed it inside a system that could expose him.

scenes.label: 49 / THE VISIT
scenes.title: The Visit
text: At 19:18, Tomas Reed received a visitor.
He was sitting at his kitchen table when the knock came.
His wife had gone to collect their youngest child from an evening lesson.
Reed had spent the last hour staring at the unsigned correction statement.
He hadn’t decided what to do.
She wore a dark coat and carried a narrow leather case.
“Because your report concerns a location that no longer exists.”
She looked past him into the house.
She moved with the quiet confidence of someone accustomed to being welcomed.
Reed led her to the kitchen.
Placed her case on the table.
The first was his incident report.
The second was the photograph he’d uploaded.
The third was a medical evaluation form.
“Mr. Reed, sometimes people encounter information that doesn’t correspond with the verified historical record.”
“Because the discrepancy may not be deliberate.”
“Then why is everyone telling me the building was demolished?”
“Because that is what the official record establishes.”
“So the record matters more than what happened?”
“No,” she said. “But records allow us to determine which accounts can be relied upon.”
“May I ask where you obtained this?”
For the first time, her expression changed.
“You’ve got the photograph. You’ve got my report. That’s enough.”
“On whether you continue to distribute unverified material.”
“It’s an explanation of the possible consequences.”
“Have you spoken to anyone outside the university about the incident?”
For a long time, he stood in the hallway.
Then he returned to the kitchen.
He looked at the unsigned correction statement.
At the photograph on his phone.
At the address Javis had given him.

scenes.label: 50 / THE WRONG PERSON
scenes.title: The Wrong Person
text: At 20:06, Liora’s terminal emitted a sharp tone.
The supplementary evidence section was empty.
Security officer reported visual confusion during routine patrol.
Liora turned the screen toward them.
The words struck harder than Javis expected.
He looked at the suspension notice.
A man who’d worked eleven years without incident.
A man who’d wanted nothing to do with their investigation.
“I told him to keep a record.”
“You didn’t tell him to upload it.”
He had believed that preserving the truth would protect Reed.
Or perhaps something worse was happening.
For the first time since discovering the correction order, he understood something about the Continuum that frightened him more than its power.
It didn’t need to erase everyone.
Sometimes it only needed to make people afraid of what they’d seen.

scenes.label: 51 / THE SECOND REPORT
scenes.title: The Second Report
text: At 21:11, a message arrived at the contact address Javis had given Reed.
Liora was the first to notice it.
I don’t know who you are, but you saw what I saw. Keep this somewhere they can’t change it.
“The signature matches the one on his employment records.”
I do not know who the people in the vehicle were. I do not know what they were carrying. I only know that the building was there, and that I saw them enter it.
Below the paragraph was another sentence.
I am writing this because I have been asked to withdraw my account. I will not sign a statement saying I imagined something I know I saw.
Reed hadn’t simply followed his advice.
He had made his own decision.
Despite everything he stood to lose.
“So preserving the truth didn’t protect him.”
For a moment, he couldn’t think of anything to say.
“But this time, we don’t act until we know who else might pay for it.”
Javis read the private statement again.
He understood that he was holding something the university could not quietly amend.
And that the man who had written it was still paying for having written it.
“Then we find out what the Continuum is going to do to him.”
“And we make sure there’s a record.”
He was silent for a moment.
“We need to find a way to protect the people who help us.”

scenes.label: 52 / WHAT THE CODEX KEPT
scenes.title: What the Codex Kept
text: Javis was alone at the workbench.
The others had gone to rest.
He hadn’t been able to sleep.
But Reed had created another record outside the system.
Something the correction hadn’t yet reached.
For a moment, he felt hope.
Preserving a record hadn’t protected the person who made it.
Javis looked down at his hand.
Of the memories he’d lost trying to preserve it.
He thought of Reed, who might now lose something far more ordinary.
For the first time, he understood why Kaelen had been so cautious.
And why Mara had destroyed her father’s machine.
Knowing something wasn’t the same as knowing what to do with it.
The Codex displayed one final line.
He could demand they find Reed.
He could try to use Weaving.
He could make another desperate attempt to save something before it disappeared.
Instead, he took out a sheet of paper.
He wrote down everything he knew about Tomas Reed.
Then he wrote one final sentence beneath it.
I will not make another decision about his life without understanding what it will cost him.
Then crossed out the last four.
I will not make another decision about his life without asking him.
Outside, the city continued as though nothing had happened.
Somewhere, Tomas Reed was facing consequences he had never agreed to.
And Javis knew that whatever happened next, he could not pretend his choices had nothing to do with it.

scenes.label: 53 / THE WINDOW
scenes.title: The Window
text: At 00:17, Javis woke Kaelen by dropping a notebook onto his chest.
“If that’s a weapon, you’re using it incorrectly.”
On the open page, he’d copied the Codex’s final message.
Kaelen swung his feet off the narrow sofa.
He stood, pulled on his jacket, and followed Javis into the workshop.
The Codex lay beneath its glass cover.
“Then we don’t know what the correction will do.”
“We know whose name appears in the record.”
“When the Continuum corrects an event, it doesn’t always remove the person involved. Sometimes it removes a statement. Sometimes an association. Sometimes a sequence of circumstances.”
“Javis, Reed isn’t necessarily about to die.”
“Then why does it say correction pending?”
“Because something connected to him hasn’t been reconciled.”
“The Continuum calls these procedures corrections because it wants them understood as repairs. But a correction is not automatically an erasure.”
“A forced attempt to make a discrepancy disappear.”
“And the discrepancy is Reed remembering Annex C.”
“You’ve become very fond of telling me what we don’t know.”
Mara stood in the doorway, wearing an oversized sweater.
“Why are you two arguing at midnight?”
“Then why are you two arguing in the morning?”
Then she pulled out a chair.
“A man might lose his memory, and that’s interesting?”
“Javis, if we misunderstand what the tablet is reporting, we might make things worse.”
“There’s no exchange record here. Only a discrepancy and a pending correction.”
“So,” Mara said, “we need to stop treating every correction as though someone has already started Weaving.”
For the first time that night, Javis considered the possibility that the Codex was warning them about something they could prevent without using his abilities.
“We find out what the Continuum wants Reed to change.”

scenes.label: 54 / THE MAN WHO SAID NO
scenes.title: The Man Who Said No
text: At 07:26, Tomas Reed answered his phone.
“I told you not to contact me again.”
“I’ve been suspended. My supervisor won’t return my calls. My wife thinks I’ve lost my mind, and a woman from a department I’ve never heard of came to my house asking for my phone.”
Kaelen was listening from the other side of the table.
“You came into my life yesterday. Since then, everything has become considerably worse.”
He could tell Reed about the correction.
But he remembered what he’d written the previous night.
“I think the people who changed your report may contact you again,” he said.
“Then I think they may try to make you withdraw your statement.”
“Listen carefully. I’m not interested in whatever conspiracy you’ve stumbled into. I don’t want to know who was in that van. I don’t want to know what they were carrying.”
The words settled heavily between them.
“No. Listen. If these people contact me again, I’ll decide what to do. You don’t come to my house. You don’t contact my family. You don’t make any arrangements on my behalf.”
Javis nodded, though Reed couldn’t see him.
“And don’t call me unless you have something that actually helps.”
“He also asked whether he was in danger.”
“Then you’ve done what he allowed you to do.”
“Is still something we need to understand.”
“Helping someone doesn’t always mean standing beside them.”

scenes.label: 55 / THE REPORT THAT WASN’T THERE
scenes.title: The Report That Wasn’t There
text: By late morning, Liora had found three versions of Reed’s incident report.
The first described an unauthorized vehicle near Annex C.
The second described visual confusion during a routine patrol.
The third claimed no incident had occurred.
“Three different records of the same shift.”
The security report had been created at 17:42.
“But Reed hadn’t even submitted the photograph at nine.”
“Each report references the same original incident number.”
“Because we received it before the latest alteration.”
“That doesn’t make it impossible to change.”
“No,” Liora agreed. “But it gives us an independently observed sequence.”
Javis looked at the three reports.
He pointed toward the Continuum extract.
“Why does this one say no incident occurred?”
“Because that’s the version they want accepted.”
Near the bottom was a reference number.
“Someone submitted an official account for reconciliation. The request is awaiting authorization.”
For the first time, the message made sense.
“But the report has already been altered.”
“So the Continuum is trying to make its preferred version official.”
“That depends on what they’re trying to correct.”
“It means they’re requesting a correction restricted to the identified discrepancy.”
“There’s one way to challenge the request.”
“Historical Verification has authority to contest a reconciliation request before approval.”
“And now we know why that matters.”
Then another line caught his attention.
“Why is the shipment record attached to Reed’s correction?”
“Because the transport record is the source of the disputed observation.”
“That means if the shipment authorization is invalid, the correction request loses part of its supporting evidence.”
“We need to see the shipment authorization.”

scenes.label: 56 / THE PRICE OF A SIGNATURE
scenes.title: The Price of a Signature
text: Liora found the shipment authorization within the hour.
It was attached to the Continuum verification extract, buried beneath three layers of administrative referral.
She placed it on the workbench.
“That’s the approval field. Look for the initiating officer.”
The approval was dated three days before the shipment notice had been created.
The same anomaly Ardent had noted.
“She was involved in the original shipment.”

“Before the Continuum centralized its reconciliation program, individual officers had authority to issue limited transfer authorizations. When the program was restructured, those authorizations were supposed to be reviewed and either confirmed or revoked.”
“Then an old authorization could still be active.”
“Can we get her to challenge it?”
“She already refused to expose her department.”
“She refused to accuse anyone. She didn’t refuse to challenge a document.”
“You’re proposing we ask her to challenge Soren’s authorization without naming her as a complainant.”
“And if she refuses, we’ve drawn attention to ourselves for nothing.”
The document felt heavier than paper had any right to.
<button class="inspect-inline" data-record="cas_shipment">[Inspect Cassius Vale Shipment Authorization]</button>
“We need to know who actually authorized the change.”
“Then we need to establish whether it can be.”
“That means the Continuum has to approve it.”
“Then we need another way to challenge the request.”
“Yes. And we need to find it before the Continuum approves the reconciliation.”

scenes.label: 57 / THE WOMAN WHO DIDN’T SIGN
scenes.title: The Woman Who Didn’t Sign
text: Dr. Selene Ardent did not answer Liora’s first message.
By the third, Liora was beginning to lose patience.
“She’s either ignoring us or someone is screening her communications.”
“If someone is monitoring her, we’re making her situation worse.”
“Is there another way to reach her?”
And he remembered something from his time there.
“Every month, the university reviews disputed historical records. Researchers can submit evidence and request an independent assessment.”
“The sessions are scheduled in advance. We didn’t create this opportunity.”
“It’s a routine review. Nothing about Annex C.”
“No forged identification. No pretending to be someone else.”
“You’re taking all the fun out of this.”
The hearing room was smaller than Javis expected.
A long table stood at the front.
Three university officials sat behind it.
Dr. Selene Ardent occupied the centre chair.
She was in her late forties, with dark hair pulled into a tight knot and the exhausted expression of someone who had spent years correcting other people’s mistakes.
Javis and Liora sat near the back.
A disagreement over the classification of a historical artefact.
The university still contained people doing ordinary work.
When the session ended, Ardent gathered her papers.
“My name is Javis. I worked in the university archives.”
“Submit an inquiry through the verification office.”
“A shipment involving the Cassius Vale investigation.”
Ardent glanced toward the remaining officials.
“Because your inquiry has already been referred.”
Javis took out a printed copy of the altered shipment notice.
Javis felt a surge of relief.
“Someone reused an authorization from another record.”
For a moment, she said nothing.
His refusal to sign a false statement.
But as she reached the door, Ardent stopped.
“There’s something you should understand about that signature.”
Ardent placed the transfer notice on the table.
“When a verification office authorizes a historical transfer, the approval is tied to a specific record. The authorization cannot legitimately be applied to another shipment.”
“But the verification system doesn’t always distinguish between the original approval and a copied reference.”
“So someone could use your signature again?”
“If they had access to the authorization record.”
“An authorization can be reused. A witness cannot.”
Ardent looked toward the empty hearing room.
“Documents can be copied, amended, or reassigned. A person who witnessed an event has an account that exists independently of those documents.”
“If you’re investigating a disputed transfer, don’t begin by asking which document is correct.”
“And if that person is being pressured to withdraw their account, you should ask why.”
“If I challenge that authorization myself, the entire verification office becomes involved. Every employee who handled the original record will be questioned.”
“I’m protecting people who had nothing to do with this.”
“But an affected party can submit a formal challenge. That would require the reviewing authority to examine the authorization without treating my department as the complainant.”
“Someone with a legitimate connection to the disputed record.”
“You said you worked in the archive.”
“Then you may already have the standing you need.”
Ardent handed him the transfer notice.
“She just told you how to challenge the authorization.”
“And made it very clear she isn’t going to do it for you.”

scenes.label: 58 / THE THING THAT SURVIVED
scenes.title: The Thing That Survived
text: Back at the workshop, Javis placed Reed’s statement beside the three conflicting reports.
“Which leaves us with a pending correction and no independent verification.”
A witness could establish what actually happened.
And an affected party could challenge a disputed authorization.
“Reed’s correction request and the Cassius shipment authorization.”
“Exactly,” Kaelen said. “The Continuum may have connected them, but we haven’t established how.”
“So challenging the shipment authorization might not stop Reed’s correction.”
Javis looked at the three reports.
“Then why does Reed’s reconciliation request reference the shipment?”
Liora opened the Continuum extract again.
“Because the disputed observation is attached to a transport record.”
“The request identifies the transport record as the source of the discrepancy.”
“So if the shipment authorization is invalid, the correction request loses part of its supporting evidence.”
“Meaning the review authority would have to reconsider it.”
“But they could still approve the correction.”
It wasn’t the answer he’d hoped for.
“Could we submit Reed’s private statement as independent evidence?”
Don’t call me unless you have something that actually helps.
He knew that waiting carried risks.
But acting without understanding them had already hurt Reed.
Javis looked at the shipment notice.
“Ardent said someone with a legitimate connection to the record could challenge it.”
“And she refused because she has people to protect.”
“So we shouldn’t ask her to expose them.”
Javis looked at the university’s public verification procedures.
“We don’t need her to accuse anyone.”
“We need the review authority to recognize that the authorization is disputed.”
“I worked in the archive. I have direct knowledge of the catalogue system. And I’ve already been identified in the original investigation.”
“You could challenge the authorization without naming Reed.”
“You told me not to make decisions about other people’s lives.”

scenes.label: 59 / THE CHALLENGE
scenes.title: The Challenge
text: At 18:42, Javis submitted a formal dispute to the university’s Historical Verification Office.
He did not mention Tomas Reed.
He did not attach the photograph.
He did not accuse the Continuum of manipulating history.
The authenticity of Dr. Selene Ardent’s authorization on the Cassius Vale shipment record.
He included the publicly available revision history.
The discrepancy between the authorization date and the document’s creation date.
And a request for independent examination.
“You haven’t made claims you can’t support.”
“Because the reconciliation request cites the disputed transport record.”
“Because the suspension only prevents approval through the disputed authorization. Someone could submit another.”
Instead, he’d managed to delay something he didn’t fully understand.
But it was more than they’d had that morning.
“I think they’re going to want to speak to me.”
For the first time, he didn’t feel the urge to run.
And whatever happened next, it was his.

scenes.label: 60 / THE NAME ON THE RECORD
scenes.title: The Name on the Record
text: Javis was standing beside Mara when the first line appeared.
“Why is it connected to Reed’s correction?”
“The reconciliation request cites the shipment as the source of Reed’s disputed observation.”
“That’s what it looks like,” Liora said.
The challenge had suspended the existing authorization.
But someone was already attempting to replace it.
He felt a familiar frustration rise.
Every time they uncovered something, the Continuum seemed to have another procedure waiting.
Then the Codex displayed one final entry.
“They haven’t found someone to authorize it.”
Liora looked toward the university records.
“Then we need to know who has that authority.”
Javis looked at the dark tablet.
And of a system that could change a person’s life with a signature.
He had spent the past two days trying to understand how the Continuum altered reality.
Now he was beginning to understand something else.
Before it changed reality, someone had to decide which version deserved to remain.
A notification sounded from Liora’s terminal.
At the top was the Continuum’s official seal.
His challenge had been accepted for preliminary review.
Because the disputed record was associated with an active reconciliation request, the person who submitted the challenge was required to provide testimony.
A line of smaller text appeared beneath the hearing instructions.
He had seen that word before.
In records that insisted he shouldn’t exist.
For two days, he’d been trying to uncover what the Continuum was hiding.
Now it was inviting him inside.
He looked toward the black tablet.
Then he looked at the clock.
Whatever happened at the hearing, he would be entering a place that had already tried to erase him.
And for the first time, he would be going there by choice.

scenes.label: 61 / TWO HOURS
scenes.title: Two Hours
text: At 21:12, Javis was still staring at the summons.
The Continuum’s seal occupied the upper-right corner of the document. Beneath it, his name appeared in plain black letters.
He read the final line again.
FAILURE TO APPEAR MAY RESULT IN DISMISSAL OF THE CHALLENGE.
“They’ve given you two hours,” Mara said.
“Two hours and eighteen minutes,” Liora corrected.
“If I don’t go, the challenge may be dismissed.”
Kaelen stood near the window, arms folded.
“You challenged an authorization. That doesn’t make you responsible for every consequence of the Continuum’s response.”
It had remained dark since the summons arrived.
“I can’t keep telling people to make their own decisions and then refuse to make mine.”
Liora turned her terminal toward them.
“The Repository’s public entrance is on the eastern side. Visitors are screened. Personal electronics are registered and held during restricted proceedings.”
“On records that couldn’t be matched to an accepted historical identity.”
Javis felt a familiar tightening in his chest.
“No,” Kaelen said. “Meaning their system doesn’t recognize the identity you’re using.”
Javis remembered the clock striking two fourteen.
Seven seconds during which he’d forgotten his own name.
Then the message on the Codex.
The cut from the archive had healed, leaving a faint line beneath the darker silver mark.
“They already took my identity,” he said. “What exactly are they verifying?”
He had spent days searching for a way into the Continuum’s records.
Now they were opening a door.
But he couldn’t ignore what lay beyond it.

scenes.label: 62 / THE CALL THAT WAS MISSED
scenes.title: The Call That Was Missed
text: The older receiver on the workbench.
The one that had carried the anonymous invitation to Station Nine.
“Because I didn’t know who was asking.”
“The one your father tried to preserve.”
“Because the cabinet was empty when I returned.”
“I wasn’t supposed to trust a stranger.”
“He trusted someone who knew how to ask the right questions.”
Mara looked toward the photograph of her father above the workbench.
Liora was already checking the receiver’s connections.
“The report was supposed to prove something. Your father discovered that the detector was identifying the wrong people.”
“It wasn’t detecting the person who caused an exchange.”
“Then you know why he was frightened.”
“He thought innocent people were being corrected.”
“Your father wrote the subject’s name on the final page.”
“And I believe someone wanted me to find it.”
“Do you think they were telling the truth?”

scenes.label: 63 / THE OLD ARCHIVIST
scenes.title: The Old Archivist
text: It came from an unfamiliar university address.
You should have spoken to me first.
Then checked the sender’s address again.
He hadn’t told Thorne where the workshop was.
But the professor had found him once before.
With two men carrying devices designed to prevent him from escaping.
Because the Continuum contacted me this afternoon.
“He asked whether I’m still at the workshop.”
Thorne answered on the second ring.
The familiar voice made something inside him tighten.
For five years, he’d heard that voice in lecture halls, archive offices, and hospital corridors.
Even after discovering the death certificate, some part of him had wanted the professor to explain everything.
“Challenging a Continuum authorization under your own name.”
“I thought my name no longer existed.”
“That’s precisely why you shouldn’t have done it.”
“Because they’ve asked me to confirm your archive access.”
“You came to the archive with two men. One had a device that could hold me in place. The other carried equipment to override the lock.”
“Those devices were intended to contain an unstable event.”
“And you still expect me to trust you?”
“That’s what you said in the archive.”
Kaelen watched the phone without moving.
“I made decisions that night I cannot justify to you over a telephone.”
“Then tell me why your name was on the case.”
“I was involved in the recovery programme.”
Something he’d seen with his own eyes.
A faint sound came through the phone.
“You told my father to hand me over.”
“Those events are not as simple as they appeared.”
“You told my father to give you the child.”
“And my mother accused you of knowing what they were going to do to me.”
“Because the explanation involves someone whose identity is still unresolved.”
Javis thought of the two children.
The smiling figure without the cut.
The voice behind the archive door.
For the first time, Thorne had admitted it.
But enough to confirm that the professor’s connection to the other child was real.
“That’s not a question I can answer for you.”
“Because I don’t trust the records that would answer it.”
He didn’t know whether that was true.
And he no longer trusted Thorne enough to believe it.
“Because the Continuum has been reviewing your university registration.”
The Continuum had retired his identity at 2:14.
He’d already seen what that meant.
“An original admission register. Attendance records. Examination results.”
“Because someone requested access to them this afternoon.”
“Because the request was not properly authorized.”
“Do you expect me to believe you’re protecting me now?”
“I want you to understand that the Continuum’s current record of you is incomplete.”
He had barely an hour before the hearing.
“An unregistered identity can still be observed. It can be questioned. It can be documented.”
“But recognition is not the same as restoration.”
“If you appear at the Repository, they may create a new record of you. That will not restore the identity they retired.”
“It will establish that someone matching your present identity appeared at a specific place and time.”
“The problem is that the Continuum already has a record of what happened to you at two fourteen.”
“If they accept both records, they will have to explain how a terminated subject can appear as a living witness.”
“It becomes yours if they decide the witness is the discrepancy.”
Javis looked down at his left hand.
“Is that what you want them to decide?”
“But I understand why you don’t believe me.”
Then another question occurred to him.
“You said someone requested my archived records.”
“They asked whether I’d ever seen you with another student who looked like you.”
“What did you tell them?” Javis asked.
“I told them I couldn’t confirm it.”
“At least we know he hasn’t suddenly become trustworthy.”
“He admitted involvement in the recovery programme.”
“And he knows about the second child.”
“Did you believe him about the archived records?”
“I don’t know whether he’s preserving evidence or keeping track of what they haven’t managed to erase.”

scenes.label: 64 / THE REPOSITORY
scenes.title: The Repository
text: At 22:58, Javis and Kaelen arrived at the Central Repository.
The building stood at the edge of the university’s administrative district, separated from the main campus by a wide avenue and a row of government offices.
Something that looked like it belonged to the people who could rewrite history.
Instead, the Repository resembled a modern records office.
A security guard reading a newspaper.
Kaelen placed the summons on the counter.
The receptionist examined the document again.
At the security desk, they surrendered their phones.
Then the guard called after him.
The guard pointed toward his hand.
The silver mark had become visible beneath his cuff.
Javis followed Kaelen toward the lift.
Neither spoke until the doors closed.
Kaelen stared at the floor indicator.
“Because we don’t know who recognizes that mark.”

scenes.label: 65 / THE FOURTH CHAIR
scenes.title: The Fourth Chair
text: Verification Chamber Four contained a long table.
Three chairs stood on one side.
A recording device sat in the centre.
A woman entered carrying a thin folder.
Javis recognized her from Reed’s description.
She placed the folder on the table.
“I understand you’ve challenged an authorization connected to a historical transfer.”
Soren looked toward the empty chairs.
“To establish whether your challenge is admissible.”
Javis looked toward the recording device.

scenes.label: 66 / THE WITNESS
scenes.title: The Witness
text: Soren placed a photograph on the table.
“Have you seen this image before?” she asked.
“I don’t think that’s relevant to my challenge.”
“Your challenge concerns the authorization of a shipment associated with the Cassius Vale investigation.”
“The shipment was originally assigned to the Central Repository. Later, the destination changed to Annex C. Then the record changed again.”
“The authorization was attributed to Dr. Selene Ardent. But the approval predates the revised shipment record.”
“Your challenge also references an archived university record.”
Javis looked at the recording device.
“Do you believe the certificate is genuine?”
“I don’t know whether it records something that happened.”
For the first time, her expression changed.
“I’ve learned not to trust easy explanations.”
Soren returned her attention to Javis.
“Your historical identity cannot be verified against the accepted record.”
“It means your testimony can be considered.”
He looked toward the recording device.
“To determine whether you’re capable of distinguishing between a genuine historical discrepancy and a memory that doesn’t belong to you.”
“Have you ever remembered something that never happened?”
The voice behind the workshop door.
“And have you ever encountered evidence that contradicted those memories?”
He understood the fear of contradictory histories.
The danger of trusting memories that might not belong to the world around him.
He understood why someone might want certainty.
A man who had seen a building.
A man whose report had been changed.
A man who had been told his own memory was unreliable.
“I understand why someone would want to investigate a contradiction.”
“But I don’t understand why the investigation begins by deciding which witness is wrong.”
“You changed Reed’s report before his reconciliation request was approved.”
He hadn’t expected him to mention Reed.
“Then why is it attached to the same shipment?”
“And you used the shipment record to question his memory.”
“If the authorization was invalid, then the evidence used against him is disputed.”
“Your challenge will remain active until the authorization is reviewed.”
“Until the review is complete, unless a new supporting authorization is accepted.”
Javis glanced at the empty chairs.
For the first time, Soren looked uncomfortable.
“Because he submitted a report that contradicted an accepted historical record.”
“Then why did you try to make him withdraw it?”
“I didn’t ask him to withdraw it.”
“You threatened him with a medical evaluation.”
“You knew what it would sound like.”
For a moment, Soren said nothing.
Then she looked down at the photograph.

scenes.label: 67 / THE EMPTY CHAIR
scenes.title: The Empty Chair
text: At 00:06, Javis and Kaelen left the hearing chamber.
Neither spoke until they reached the corridor.
“Because he asked you not to involve him.”
“You still identified your connection to him.”
“You made a choice that could affect him.”
“Then what was I supposed to do?”
“But uncertainty doesn’t remove the consequences of a decision.”
Javis looked back toward the hearing room.
“Preliminary hearings don’t always require a full panel.”
“She requested Reed’s reconciliation. Then she reviewed the challenge to the authorization supporting it.”
“Did the summons identify her as the reviewer?”
“Javis, listen carefully. If Soren was assigned to review a challenge involving her own request, someone either ignored the safeguards or deliberately arranged it.”
Javis looked back toward the hearing room.
As the doors closed, Javis glanced toward the corridor one last time.
She simply watched until the doors shut.

scenes.label: 68 / THE RECORD THAT REMAINED
scenes.title: The Record That Remained
text: At 00:41, Javis returned to Mara’s workshop.
Liora was asleep at the terminal.
Mara sat beside the Codex, examining an old circuit board.
When he finished, Mara was quiet.
Javis looked down at his hand.
A new line appeared beneath the original archive entry.
“His presence at the hearing has been recorded.”
For days, he’d been living with the knowledge that his identity had been retired.
His university records had begun disappearing.
The Continuum’s systems no longer recognized the life he’d lived.
Now, an official record acknowledged that someone calling himself Javis had appeared before its representatives.
“Does that mean they can’t erase me?”
“Be careful what you conclude from that.”
“They’ve acknowledged your appearance. They haven’t restored your identity.”
Recognition is not the same as restoration.
“So they can accept that I stood in that room without accepting that I have a history.”
“And if the Continuum decides the contradiction is dangerous?”
The mystery of the two children remained.
And somewhere, Professor Thorne still possessed records of a life he’d helped the Continuum take away.
Mara looked toward the dark tablet.
Of the two children standing in the white room.
And of Thorne, who had known both of them long before Javis had known his name.
He looked toward the workshop window.
Outside, the city continued as though nothing extraordinary had happened.
And somewhere, someone was deciding which version of history deserved to remain.
Javis looked back at the others.
“Now,” he said, “we find out what happened to the people they corrected.”
“And what happened to the other child.”

scenes.label: 69 / THE ORIGINAL
scenes.title: The Original
text: The first thing Javis noticed was the handwriting.
Professor Thorne had always written the number seven with a short line through its stem. He claimed it was an old habit from his years working with European archival systems.
Javis had seen it on examination papers, research notes, scholarship recommendations, and the occasional birthday card.
Now it appeared on the margin of a document that should not have existed.
Beneath the heading were two entries.
Both carried the same date of birth.
Both had been signed by Aris Thorne.
But the identification numbers were different.
Javis examined the page without speaking.
Liora stood beside him at the workshop table. She had spent the better part of an hour comparing the document against the surviving university records.
“With Thorne’s handwriting. That doesn’t prove he signed both entries, but there’s no obvious indication of forgery.”
One entry had been crossed out.
“That depends on whether these records were created before or after the correction.”
He returned his attention to the page.
There was something deeply unsettling about seeing his existence reduced to two administrative entries.
He thought of the memory spindle.
Two children standing in a white room.
They told your parents there could only be one.
“Perhaps someone wanted proof that the second entry existed.”
He looked at the signature again.
The man who had helped raise him.
The man who had chased him through the university archives.
The man who had apparently supervised sixteen attempts to recover him.
“Something I should have done a long time ago.”

scenes.label: 70 / THE PROFESSOR
scenes.title: The Professor
text: Thorne answered on the third ring.
“There are two entries. Same name. Same birth date. Different identification numbers.”
“That’s a strange thing to say after the university archive.”
“One of them nearly immobilized me with an anchor.”
“Did you supervise sixteen attempts to erase me?”
For five years, Javis had trusted this man.
He remembered arriving at the university with a scholarship that barely covered his expenses.
Thorne had found him additional work.
When Javis’s research application was rejected, Thorne had encouraged him to try again.
When Javis was hospitalized after an accident, Thorne had visited every evening for a week.
None of those memories had disappeared.
That was what made this difficult.
The admission hurt more than he’d expected.
“By preventing them from finding the wrong person.”
“The old preservation laboratory. North of the botanical gardens.”
It had been closed for years.
“You don’t get to make that request anymore.”
“Bring someone you trust. But don’t bring the Codex.”
“Because the last time it entered a room with both of you, someone died.”

scenes.label: 71 / SOMEONE ELSE REMEMBERS
scenes.title: Someone Else Remembers
text: Mara was the first to object.
Javis placed his phone on the table.
Kaelen stood beside the workshop entrance, examining the lock.
“Because we’ve spent days investigating what happened to me while avoiding the person who was there.”
“There’s a reason we avoided him,” Mara said.
“He brought the Continuum to your parents.”
“He tried to take you from Elara.”
“But I also know he could have handed me over at any point during the five years I worked for him.”
“Either he spent five years protecting me from something, or he spent five years making sure I was where the Continuum wanted me.”
“And you think he’ll tell you which?”
Javis picked up the admission record.
“I think he’ll tell me something I can verify.”
YOU SHOULD ASK HIM ABOUT THE WHITE ROOM.
Javis felt a familiar coldness settle in his stomach.
“Would you believe me if I did?”
“I don’t know which name you’d recognize.”
Javis felt the workshop recede around him.
“Because we weren’t supposed to remain together.”
The voice behind the archive door had known about it.
The smiling figure in the photograph hadn’t possessed it.
“Were you the one outside the archive?” Javis asked.
“You told me not to let you in.”
“Not in the room with you. Not physically.”
The image of himself standing behind his own desk.
“The borrowing slip. The warning about Thorne. The maintenance key.”
“Then why should I believe any of this?”
“Because there’s something Thorne hasn’t told you.”
“When you enter the preservation laboratory, look beneath the examination table.”
“There should be a narrow compartment under the left side. Inside is a brass identification plate.”
“I want you to read it yourself.”
“Because if I tell you, you’ll think I invented it.”
“The reason Thorne kept one of us.”

scenes.label: 72 / THE LABORATORY
scenes.title: The Laboratory
text: The old preservation laboratory stood behind a line of overgrown hedges.
A rusted sign identified it as a former university research facility.
Javis remembered visiting the building once as a student.
Thorne had brought him there to collect damaged manuscripts from a storage room.
At least, that was what Javis remembered.
He stood outside the entrance with Kaelen.
“You’re certain you want to do this?” Kaelen asked.
“People who are certain tend to make expensive mistakes.”
Kaelen checked the small instrument concealed inside his jacket.
The replacement wasn’t as powerful as the rod he’d destroyed at the records office.
Liora and Mara remained at the workshop, maintaining contact through an ordinary audio connection.
Nothing that would announce their arrival.
Javis pushed open the laboratory door.
The interior smelled of damp plaster and old chemicals.
Their footsteps echoed through the corridor.
At the end stood a room illuminated by a single lamp.
Professor Thorne waited beside a metal table.
He looked older than Javis remembered.
The professor’s gaze moved to Kaelen.
The metal table stood between them.
He noticed the restraints attached to its sides.
The answer had come too easily.
Two observation windows, their glass clouded with age.
The room from Haziah’s recording had been white.
This room had once been white too.
He could see the paint beneath the stains.
“I saw you in my mother’s memory.”
“Then stop telling me you were protecting us.”
For the first time, he seemed genuinely afraid of answering.
Thorne looked toward the examination table.
“The one your parents asked me to keep.”

scenes.label: 73 / THE PLATE
scenes.title: The Plate
text: Javis felt something settle into place.
He crouched beside the examination table and examined its underside.
A narrow compartment lay beneath the left edge.
Exactly where the caller had said.
Inside lay a small brass plate.
The surface was tarnished, but the engraved letters remained legible.
Beneath the classifications were two identification numbers.
The numbers from the admission register.
He turned the plate toward the light.
The active university entry matched Subject A.
The crossed-out entry matched Subject B.
Javis stared at the man who had raised him.
“Because your parents believed that was the only way to save both.”
“No. My mother was trying to stop you.”
“She was trying to stop what happened afterward.”
Thorne looked at the brass plate.
“Both children survived,” Thorne said. “But the process had already begun treating them as a single continuity.”
Javis looked down at the identification numbers.
“The Continuum’s system could recognize two bodies. It could not reliably preserve two histories attached to the same originating identity.”
“Those weren’t sixteen attempts to kill me.”
“They were attempts to remove the other one.”
“Giving me half an answer whenever the truth becomes uncomfortable.”
“The first correction was intended to separate your histories. It failed. Every subsequent attempt was supposed to repair the damage caused by the previous one.”
He had assumed they all showed him.
But the records had never carried a surname.
A name assigned to a continuity.
“How many of those photographs were actually me?”

scenes.label: 74 / WHAT THORNE CHOSE
scenes.title: What Thorne Chose
text: Then Javis asked the question he’d been avoiding.
Thorne looked toward the dark observation window.
“They didn’t know the Continuum intended to use the children to test a permanent correction.”
“I believed the alternative would destroy them both.”
The place where two children had been reduced to an experiment.
“Did you tell my mother what you suspected?”
Thorne had decided what Elara was allowed to know.
Just as he’d spent years deciding what Javis was allowed to know.
The admission hung in the room.
“Then why did you keep working for them?”
“The difference is that I was trying to recover the child they had taken.”
For the first time, the professor’s voice broke.
“I signed the first transfer. I helped them take him. And when I discovered what they were doing, I tried to bring him back.”
“Because they needed someone who could identify the original subjects.”
Javis looked at the brass plate.
“That’s why you stayed close to me.”
“To make sure they never mistook you for him.”
The command not to touch the Codex.
“The Continuum received confirmation that the second subject had regained access to the original record.”
“Then why did you come after me?”
“The men I brought were supposed to contain the artifact and prevent another transfer.”
“You ordered them to override the door.”
“After five years of lying to me?”
Javis placed the brass plate on the table.
“Then you should have told me the truth five years ago.”
For once, he offered no explanation.

scenes.label: 75 / THE WRONG CHILD
scenes.title: The Wrong Child
text: Kaelen pointed to the identification numbers.
“Subject A was retained. Subject B was transferred.”
“And the active university record belongs to Subject A.”
“Then why does Case 0017 identify him as the subject scheduled for termination?”
“If the Continuum was trying to recover Subject B, why would the termination record be attached to Subject A?”
The older man stared at the brass plate.
Thorne looked at the identification numbers again.
“The active university entry should belong to the child I retained.”
“Not if the termination record is correct.”
The request struck him with unexpected force.
Mara had asked the same thing.
The other voice had known about the cut.
The photographs had shown different hands.
His legs seemed to give way beneath him.
Thorne looked at the brass plate.
“The records were corrected. I knew that. I preserved the original register because I believed I could still distinguish the two of you.”
Thorne continued, barely above a whisper.
“I don’t know whether you were the one I saved.”

scenes.label: 76 / THE TEST
scenes.title: The Test
text: He wanted to walk out of the laboratory, return to the workshop, and put as much distance as possible between himself and the professor.
Instead, he remained beside the examination table.
He thought of the phone call.
The reason Thorne kept one of us.
The caller had known about the compartment.
He’d known something even Thorne seemed unable to reconcile.
“I’m going to ask you one question.”
“When I was seven, I had an accident.”
“And you refused to tell anyone because you thought I’d stop letting you visit the gardens.”
Thorne carrying him to the infirmary.
“You kept the broken watch I gave you that morning. Even after it stopped working.”
He had kept it for years.
“You left it with me before your final examination. You said you’d collect it afterward.”
He remembered giving Thorne something before the examination.
He remembered asking the professor to keep it safe.
He remembered opening the watch as a child.
But he remembered tracing them with his thumb.
“The caller said the other child was transferred.”
“But some of my memories don’t match his.”
Javis looked down at the brass plate.
“Then we need something neither of them can rewrite.”
Javis held the plate between them.
“You don’t get to keep the evidence anymore.”
They had almost reached the corridor when Thorne spoke again.
The professor stood beside the examination table.
“Whatever you discover about which child you were…”
Javis looked at him for a long moment.
“It changes what you did to the other one.”

scenes.label: 77 / THE MAN WHO WAITED
scenes.title: The Man Who Waited
text: The laboratory door was open when Javis arrived.

He stopped beneath the entrance canopy, listening. Somewhere beyond the overgrown grounds, a delivery truck changed gears. The air was warm and still, carrying the smell of cut grass from the university gardens.
Kaelen stood beside him, studying the building.
“Thorne called seventeen minutes ago,” he said. “If he wanted to trap us, he’s had enough time to prepare something considerably better than an open door.”
“I’m trying to establish what kind of trouble we’re walking into.”
Kaelen took a compact instrument from his jacket. Its blue indicator brightened as he pointed it toward the entrance.
Javis recognized the device. He had seen Kaelen use it before, though he’d never been particularly interested in how it worked.
“Active anchors. Some residual exchanges. Depends on the equipment.”
“There’s an anchor operating inside. Old configuration. Stronger than it should be.”
“Probably. Whether that’s a good idea is another question.”
A voice drifted from the corridor.
“I’ve been waiting longer than seventeen minutes.”
The corridor was dim, but the examination room ahead glowed with a steady white light.
Professor Thorne stood near the observation window.
His glasses were missing. A shallow cut crossed his cheek, and his right hand was wrapped in a bloodstained handkerchief.
Beside the examination table stood another man.
He had seen his own face in photographs, mirrors, recordings, and impossible glimpses through locked doors.
None of those experiences prepared him for seeing it turn toward him.
The stranger was slightly thinner. His hair was longer, and he held his shoulders differently, as though expecting someone to approach from behind.
The stranger studied him with an expression Javis couldn’t interpret.
It was a small, spontaneous sound.
For some reason, that disturbed Javis more than the resemblance.
Javis took another step into the room.
“Were you the one outside the archive?”
He’d imagined this meeting as a confrontation. He’d expected accusations, perhaps violence.
Instead, he found himself struggling with an absurd question.
How did you introduce yourself to someone who already had your face?
The name settled somewhere uncomfortable in Javis’s memory.
He had encountered its beginning before, in a fragment he couldn’t place.
“Because I got tired of answering to yours.”
“You can imagine how inconvenient that became.”

scenes.label: 78 / THE CHILD THORNE REMEMBERED
scenes.title: The Child Thorne Remembered
text: “Javis, before you listen to anything he tells you—”
“Five years to explain what happened. You had considerably longer with me, although our conversations were less pleasant.”
“You know why I couldn’t tell him.”
He was accustomed to people obeying when he raised his voice in anger. Seeing his own face respond with the same instinct made him feel strangely exposed.
“You told me you kept one child and surrendered the other.”
“You also told me you couldn’t be certain which one you raised.”
Aren walked to the examination table and sat on its edge.
“The one you fell through when you were seven.”
Javis felt a familiar tightening in his wrist.
He remembered the glass breaking beneath him.
Thorne carrying him through a corridor while someone shouted for a doctor.
A thin white scar ran along the inside of his wrist.
Javis looked down at his own.
Kaelen approached, examining both arms without touching them.
The professor stared at the floor.
“I treated the injury. I signed the hospital forms. I remember taking the child home.”
“Professor, you were there. Surely you can remember something that distinguishes us.”
Thorne reached toward the brass plate Javis had brought from the workshop.
“The original register distinguished two subjects. I preserved it because I believed the identification numbers would remain reliable.”
“After the corrections, some records showed one subject. Others showed two. Occasionally, the records agreed while my memories contradicted them.”
Aren leaned back against the table.
“Sometimes he remembered things you did with me.”

scenes.label: 79 / THE FIRST CORRECTION
scenes.title: The First Correction
text: Javis pulled a chair away from the wall and sat.
He was tired of standing in rooms where everyone else appeared to know more about his life.
“I know Cassius brought Elara into this reality through Weaving. I know the Continuum eventually corrected that displacement.”
“Elara was returned to her originating reality.”
“Your mother had a history in another reality. Your father had a history here. The Continuum understood how to reverse the transfer that brought Elara across.”
“You had been born here,” Thorne continued, “but the history that made your birth possible wasn’t confined to this reality.”
Kaelen looked up from his instrument.
“And the correction model only accounted for the local history.”
“After they started getting results they couldn’t explain.”
“The initial operation returned Elara. It didn’t remove Javis.”
Aren’s fingers tightened around the edge of the table.
The professor’s silence was an answer, but Javis wanted more than an admission.
Thorne looked toward the observation window.
“The subject disappeared. His registered history was removed. The remaining records no longer supported his existence.”
Aren was staring at his hands.
“That was how long they thought they’d finished the job.”
“Then a child appeared at a Continuum monitoring station.”
“The first return had already been registered as the restoration of the original subject. When the second appeared, the system identified a competing continuity.”
The first correction had erased the child.
But something remained beyond the history the Continuum had altered.
And when that history asserted itself again, the system had already accepted another continuation.
Javis thought about the photographs in Case 0017.
He had assumed the Continuum had failed sixteen times to erase one person.
Now he understood why that explanation had never quite fitted the evidence.
“What happened after the two children appeared?”

scenes.label: 80 / THE RECORD OF SUCCESS
scenes.title: The Record of Success
text: Kaelen had been silent for several minutes.
Now he crossed the room and placed his instrument on the examination table.
“Professor, I want the original correction logs.”
“I’m standing in a laboratory with two men carrying the same historical identity. I think we’ve moved beyond ordinary classification concerns.”
The professor looked sharply at him.
Kaelen pointed toward the wall cabinet.
“Third panel. Lower compartment. The wiring behind it is still live.”
“Haziah taught me to recognize Continuum field installations.”
“He didn’t need to. Your equipment follows the same architecture.”
“Unless you’ve redesigned the entire system, there’s a local audit unit behind that panel. It records anchor activations even when the central logs are unavailable.”
“Are you going to open it, or should I?”
After a long pause, Thorne stood.
He removed a narrow key from his pocket.
The cabinet opened with a metallic click.
Behind the third panel sat a compact terminal.
Several carried warnings about unresolved exchange debt.
Beneath it was another entry, dated several weeks later.
The Continuum had successfully removed individual continuities.
It had never resolved the underlying connection.
“You knew the corrections were locally successful. Your reports called the later appearances new deviations.”
“You treated every return as a new failure requiring another correction. But you never established whether the original correction could eliminate the source.”
“The source was an unresolved cross-reality origin.”
“And you kept applying corrections within one reality.”
“We had no way to access the other.”
“Then you had no basis for believing the next attempt would work.”
“We were trying to prevent further instability.”
“By repeating the operation that produced it?”
Kaelen stepped back from the terminal.
Javis had never heard him speak to Thorne with such contempt.
“He warned you that correction records measured the result of an operation, not the full consequences.”
Kaelen turned the screen toward Javis.
Each successful removal was followed by an unregistered return.
Then something else caught his attention.
During several intervals, records indicated that one continuity had remained active while the other was absent.
“And there were times you were here while I was gone.”
The memories that no longer fitted together.

“The corrections were repeatedly attempting to reconcile two histories against the same originating identity. When a continuity returned, the system couldn’t always restore its memories independently.”
“So it gave us pieces of each other.”
Javis looked at the scar on his wrist.
Thorne carrying a child through the corridor.
A memory he’d trusted his entire life.
He couldn’t tell whether he’d experienced it.
“And this is why Thorne couldn’t identify which child he raised.”
The professor’s face had gone grey.
For years, he’d relied on memories and records that the correction process itself had compromised.
He had tried to distinguish two lives using evidence that no longer reliably belonged to either.

scenes.label: 81 / THE THINGS THAT REMAIN
scenes.title: The Things That Remain
text: Aren moved away from the terminal.
“Very tidy. You could write a paper about it.”
“I spent four months in a room without windows because they thought I was a memory that hadn’t been properly removed.”
“Do you remember a woman named Tessa?”
“She worked at one of the facilities. She used to bring me books.”
“She hated the endings. Said the heroes always survived because the writers were cowards.”
“She was the first person who told me I wasn’t a mistake.”
“They questioned her because she kept using my name after a correction.”
Javis thought of the list Aren had mentioned over the telephone.
The witnesses who had become inconvenient.
“A woman standing beside a bed. She gave me a book.”
Her hand resting on a book.
For several seconds, he said nothing.
Neither knew whose memory had come first.
The uncertainty might once have frightened him.
Now, looking at Aren, he found something else beneath it.
For a woman neither could locate.
For childhoods neither could fully claim.
For the years they’d spent existing in the spaces left by each other’s disappearance.
“I knew there was someone living outside those facilities. Someone with my face who could go to school, have friends, complain about ordinary things.”
But he couldn’t find an apology that wouldn’t sound like he was asking forgiveness for having lived.
Instead, he pulled out the chair beside Aren.

scenes.label: 82 / THE PROFESSOR’S FAILURE
scenes.title: The Professor’s Failure
text: Javis watched him for a while.
Then asked, “When did you realize there were two of us?”
“And when did you realize the corrections could erase either one?”
“I believed that if I remained, I could influence what happened to you.”
“You told them which memories to test.”
“Then stop talking as though you were merely watching.”
“I helped create the recovery programme. I believed we could restore a stable history without losing either of you.”
“I knew the corrections could remove a continuity.”
“By then, the returns had become predictable enough that—”
Aren struck the examination table with his palm.
The sound echoed through the room.
“Do you know what it feels like to remember dying?”
“I remember a corridor collapsing around me. I remember drowning. I remember waking somewhere else with people telling me none of it happened.”
“I remember being afraid to sleep because I didn’t know whether I’d wake up in the same life.”
Aren stopped a few feet away.
“And every time, you wrote another report.”
The words seemed to anger him more than another excuse would have.
“You don’t get to make that sound sufficient.”
He had wanted Thorne to admit what he’d done.
Now that he had, the admission seemed painfully small beside the consequences.
“To the people you’ve spent years telling what happened.”
“This time, you’re going to tell them what you actually know.”

scenes.label: 83 / KAELEN’S DECISION
scenes.title: Kaelen’s Decision
text: Kaelen had begun copying the audit files to a portable storage unit.
Kaelen entered a sequence of commands.
Kaelen glanced toward the laboratory door.
“Javis, these are the original recovery logs. We have spent days relying on altered records and secondhand testimony.”
“Then you know why we need them.”
“And I know what happens when the Continuum decides someone has become inconvenient.”
For a moment, his expression became unreadable.
Then he said, “I helped prepare one of these operations.”
Kaelen kept his eyes on the screen.
“A family was displaced after an unauthorized transfer. The Continuum wanted the affected history reconciled.”
“I reviewed the field data. There were inconsistencies, but the system classified the correction as successful.”
“Later, someone reported remembering a child who wasn’t in the restored records.”
Kaelen looked toward the audit entries.
“I accepted the report because it matched what I’d been taught to expect. Haziah challenged the underlying assumptions. I thought he was being reckless.”
“I’ve been wondering what else I helped them overlook.”
Kaelen turned back to the terminal.
“If I leave these records here, I make the same decision again.”
“You’ve just told them where you are.”
“I spent years trusting the wrong evidence. I’m finished hiding behind that.”
Then the terminal emitted a sharp tone.
Kaelen slipped the device into his jacket.
“Now we have something worth leaving with.”

scenes.label: 84 / THE ANCHOR
scenes.title: The Anchor
text: They were preparing to leave when Aren stumbled.
The other man’s skin was cold.
Silver lines had appeared along his neck.
Thorne moved toward the wall panel.
“It’s maintaining a local continuity reference,” Thorne said. “Aren’s presence here is being held against the last stable record.”
“Not safely while the anchor is active.”
“We don’t know what happens when the reference disappears.”
“I know what happens if I stay.”
Javis remembered the Continuum’s correction records.
Histories that could disappear without their underlying origin being resolved.
“Will switching it off erase him?” Javis asked.
“I can’t determine that from this instrument.”
“The anchor may be preventing an uncontrolled displacement.”
“And it may be keeping me exactly where they want me.”
For once, he had no patience for anyone pretending certainty.
“The anchor isn’t performing a correction. It’s holding a reference to a particular continuity state.”
“Meaning it can help keep Aren here. But it isn’t the source of his existence.”
Kaelen pointed toward a second indicator concealed beneath the housing.
“This is a remote monitoring channel. It’s been active since the anchor was engaged.”
“They know someone is here. Whether they know exactly who depends on what the system has reported.”
“And you knew about the monitoring channel?”
There was nothing left to say.
“I can isolate the transmitter without disabling the anchor. It may buy us time.”
This time, he managed several steps before the silver marks brightened.
“His continuity is fluctuating beyond the anchor’s effective range.”
“And now we’ve cut their monitoring channel, they’ll know something happened.”
“Possibly. Nightingale was designed to detect exchange consequences. Cassius’s modifications may have made it capable of distinguishing repeated continuity signatures.”
“You’re talking about me as though I’m equipment.”
“I’ve spent enough of my life waiting for people to decide when I’m stable.”
“Then we find a way to get you out. But I’m not going to pretend I know how.”

scenes.label: 85 / THE COST OF A NAME
scenes.title: The Cost of a Name
text: “The anchor is referencing a historical identity. If we can establish a separate reference for Aren, we might be able to move him without forcing the system to treat him as Javis.”
“The records don’t support an independent continuity.”
Kaelen glanced toward the storage unit.
“You submitted evidence that two subjects existed.”
“And the Continuum acknowledged a secondary subject.”
“That means there’s already a disputed record outside this laboratory.”
“Javis? We’ve been trying to reach you.”
“Two active subjects confirmed. The custody record is still restricted.”
“This may be enough to establish a temporary reference.”
“We’re not rewriting anyone’s history. We’re using the existing acknowledgment that a second subject is present.”
“Potentially the anchor’s current reference. We’d have to disconnect it from the shared identity.”
“If the system can’t maintain two references, it may reject one.”
The Continuum had acknowledged both, but it hadn’t recognized them as independent people.
“We need the original custody record to prove their histories diverged.”
“Shows two subjects. It doesn’t establish where each continuity went after the corrections.”
“They establish alternating removals and returns. Some entries are incomplete.”
He removed the small brass watch and placed it on the table.
Thorne had claimed to have given it to him.
Aren had said it belonged to both of them.
“Then how can it be engraved on a watch from our childhood?”
For several seconds, he said nothing.
“I remember Mother giving it to us.”
“But you chose the name Aren later.”
The memory was genuine to Aren.
That didn’t mean the event had happened as he remembered it.
The correction process had entangled their histories.
Perhaps the watch had belonged to a different version of their childhood.
“Not as proof of which history came first.”
He examined the watch more closely.
“But we can preserve it as evidence that the histories don’t agree.”
Aren was still staring at the engraving.
“I thought I remembered everything about this.”
Then Aren closed the watch and placed it between them.
“I don’t know which memories are mine.”

scenes.label: 86 / THE ROOM BEHIND THE GLASS
scenes.title: The Room Behind the Glass
text: Javis remembered his father standing behind the glass.
Not clearly. The image kept shifting whenever he tried to examine it.
Sometimes there was a child beside him.
And sometimes Javis remembered being the child, looking through the glass at someone who had his face.
He sat on the examination table, pressing his fingers against his temples.
Across from him, Aren was staring at the observation window.
Kaelen stood beside the terminal, studying the residual reading from the exchange.
The instrument had detected a cross-reality signature. Whatever caused it had already passed.
Thorne watched him from the doorway.
“The anchor registered no exchange. That doesn’t rule out an interaction.”
“I haven’t established that anything physical crossed.”
“It’s possible the exchange affected what you remembered. But neither of you should assume the memory belongs to the person experiencing it.”
He turned the terminal toward them.
The maintenance archive contained a record that hadn’t appeared in the recovery logs.
“Your father helped develop the early preservation equipment.”
Thorne looked toward the observation window.
It showed the examination room, the observation window, the anchor—
And another chamber behind the wall.
Aren stared at the wall beneath the observation window.
Aren ran his hand along the wall.
“I remember someone bringing me through this passage.”
For several seconds, he seemed to be listening to something.
Then he pressed a narrow section of the wall.
Beyond it, a narrow corridor disappeared into darkness.

scenes.label: 87 / CASSIUS’S ROOM
scenes.title: Cassius’s Room
text: The corridor smelled of dust and old insulation.
Kaelen led the way with a small lamp.
Exposed cables ran along the ceiling. Faded yellow paint marked the floor.
The passage ended at a metal door.
Its identification plate had been removed.
“I remember being told not to open it.”
“The room was sealed after he disappeared.”
“After he stopped reporting to the Continuum.”
“I don’t know where your father went.”
The room beyond was surprisingly ordinary.
A narrow shelf holding old notebooks.
A wall of obsolete monitoring equipment.
Beside the desk stood a child’s wooden stool.
Javis stopped when he saw it.
He remembered sitting on something like that.
His feet swinging above the floor.
The stool creaked beneath his weight.
For a moment, Javis almost laughed.
It was pinned beneath a cracked sheet of plastic.
Three figures stood beneath an enormous yellow sun.
He remembered drawing a sun like that.
Several notebooks lay beneath a protective cover.
The pages contained diagrams of overlapping circles, measurements, and handwritten calculations.
“Your father was investigating how a transferred history remained connected to its originating reality.”
Several pages had been crossed out.
Others contained questions written in the margins.
Can a transferred history remain independently active?
What survives when the local record does not?
Javis found a sealed envelope beneath the notebooks.
Four words were written across it.
Kaelen stepped away from the desk.
His father’s handwriting stared back at him.
For years, Javis had imagined what he might say if he ever found Cassius.
He had never considered that Cassius might have something to say first.

scenes.label: 88 / THE LETTER
scenes.title: The Letter
text: The envelope contained a single folded sheet.
The handwriting was uneven in places, as though Cassius had written quickly.
I don’t know whether this letter will ever reach you.
There are things I should have told you while I still had the chance.
I know that sounds like a small explanation for something that changed so many lives. Perhaps it is.
When I brought Elara into my reality, I believed I understood what I was doing. I knew there would be consequences. I convinced myself I could manage them.
You used to sit beside my desk and ask why the lights inside my instruments changed colour.
I told you they were measuring things too small for us to see.
